#10882. Llama can now see and run on your device - welcome Llama 3.2

Llama 3.2 is out! Today, we welcome the next iteration of the Llama collection to Hugging Face. This time, we’re excited to collaborate with Meta on the release of multimodal and small models. Ten open-weight models (5 multimodal models and 5 text-only ones) are available on the Hub.

Llama 3.2 Vision comes in two sizes: 11B for efficient deployment and development on consumer-size GPU, and 90B for large-scale applications. Both versions come in base and instruction-tuned variants. In addition to the four multimodal models, Meta released a new version of Llama Guard with vision support. Llama Guard 3 is a safeguard model that can classify model inputs and generations, including detecting harmful multimodal prompts or assistant responses.

Llama 3.2 also includes small text-only language models that can run on-device. They come in two new sizes (1B and 3B) with base and instruct variants, and they have strong capabilities for their sizes. There’s also a small 1B version of Llama Guard that can be deployed alongside these or the larger text models in production use cases.

Among the features and integrations being released, we have:

Llama 3.2 Vision is the most powerful open multimodal model released by Meta. It has great visual understanding and reasoning capabilities and can be used to accomplish a variety of tasks, including visual reasoning and grounding, document question answering, and image-text retrieval. Chain of Thought (CoT) answers are often very good, which makes visual reasoning particularly powerful.

Llama 3.2 Vision can be used to process text and an image as well as only text. With image-text prompting, the model can take English inputs, while for text-only prompting, the model can handle multiple languages.

The full list of languages in text-only mode is:

The architecture of these models is based on the combination of Llama 3.1 LLMs combined with a vision tower and an image adapter. The text models used are Llama 3.1 8B for the Llama 3.2 11B Vision model, and Llama 3.1 70B for the 3.2 90B Vision model. To the best of our understanding, the text models were frozen during the training of the vision models to preserve text-only performance.

Below you can find some inference examples from the 11B instruction-tuned model that showcase real world knowledge, document reasoning and infographics understanding capabilities.

Vision models have a context length of 128k tokens, which allows for multiple-turn conversations that may contain images. However, the model works best when attending to a single image, so the transformers implementation only attends to the last image provided in the input. This preserves quality and saves memory.

The 11B base model supports tile sizes of 448, while the instruct version and the 90B models all use tile sizes of 560. The models were trained on a massive dataset of 6 billion image-text pairs with a diverse data mixture. This makes them excellent candidates for fine-tuning on downstream tasks. For reference, you can see below how the 11B, 90B and their instruction fine-tuned versions compare in some benchmarks, as reported by Meta. Please, refer to the model cards for additional benchmarks and details.

We expect the text capabilities of these models to be on par with the 8B and 70B Llama 3.1 models, respectively, as our understanding is that the text models were frozen during the training of the Vision models. Hence, text benchmarks should be consistent with 8B and 70B.

Regarding the licensing terms, Llama 3.2 comes with a very similar license to Llama 3.1, with one key difference in the acceptable use policy: any individual domiciled in, or a company with a principal place of business in, the European Union is not being granted the license rights to use multimodal models included in Llama 3.2. This restriction does not apply to end users of a product or service that incorporates any such multimodal models, so people can still build global products with the vision variants.

For full details, please make sure to read the official license and acceptable use policy.

The Llama 3.2 collection includes 1B and 3B text models. These models are designed for on-device use cases, such as prompt rewriting, multilingual knowledge retrieval, summarization tasks, tool usage, and locally running assistants. They outperform many of the available open-access models at these sizes and compete with models that are many times larger. In a later section, we’ll show you how to run these models offline.

The models follow the same architecture as Llama 3.1. They were trained with up to 9 trillion tokens and still support the long context length of 128k tokens. The models are multilingual, supporting English, German, French, Italian, Portuguese, Hindi, Spanish, and Thai.

There is also a new small version of Llama Guard, Llama Guard 3 1B, that can be deployed with these models to evaluate the last user or assistant responses in a multi-turn conversation. It uses a set of pre-defined categories which (new to this version) can be customized or excluded to account for the developer’s use case. For more details on the use of Llama Guard, please refer to the model card.

Bonus: Llama 3.2 has been exposed to a broader collection of languages than the 8 supported languages mentioned above. Developers are encouraged to fine-tune Llama 3.2 models for their specific language use cases.

We ran the base models through the Open LLM Leaderboard evaluation suite, while the instruct models were evaluated across three popular benchmarks that measure instruction-following and correlate well with the LMSYS Chatbot Arena: IFEval, AlpacaEval, and MixEval-Hard. These are the results for the base models, with Llama-3.1-8B included as a reference:

And here are the results for the instruct models, with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct included as a reference:

Remarkably, the 3B model is as strong as the 8B one on IFEval! This makes the model well-suited for agentic applications, where following instructions is crucial for improving reliability. This high IFEval score is very impressive for a model of this size.

Tool use is supported in both the 1B and 3B instruction-tuned models. Tools are specified by the user in a zero-shot setting (the model has no previous information about the tools developers will use). Thus, the built-in tools that were part of the Llama 3.1 models (brave_search and wolfram_alpha) are no longer available.

Due to their size, these small models can be used as assistants for bigger models and perform assisted generation (also known as speculative decoding). Here is an example of using the Llama 3.2 1B model as an assistant to the Llama 3.1 8B model. For offline use cases, please check the on-device section later in the post.

You can experiment with the three Instruct models in the following demos:

The text-only checkpoints have the same architecture as previous releases, so there is no need to update your environment. However, given the new architecture, Llama 3.2 Vision requires an update to Transformers. Please make sure to upgrade your installation to release 4.45.0 or later.

Once upgraded, you can use the new Llama 3.2 models and leverage all the tools of the Hugging Face ecosystem.

You can run the 1B and 3B Text model checkpoints in just a couple of lines with Transformers. The model checkpoints are uploaded in bfloat16 precision, but you can also use float16 or quantized weights. Memory requirements depend on the model size and the precision of the weights. Here's a table showing the approximate memory required for inference using different configurations:

We load the model in bfloat16. As mentioned above, this is the type used by the original checkpoint published by Meta, so it’s the recommended way to run to ensure the best precision or conduct evaluations. Depending on your hardware, float16 might be faster.

By default, transformers uses the same sampling parameters (temperature=0.6 and top_p=0.9) as the original meta codebase. We haven’t conducted extensive tests yet, feel free to explore!

The Vision models are larger, so they require more memory to run than the small text models. For reference, the 11B Vision model takes about 10 GB of GPU RAM during inference, in 4-bit mode.

The easiest way to infer with the instruction-tuned Llama Vision model is to use the built-in chat template. The inputs have user and assistant roles to indicate the conversation turns. One difference with respect to the text models is that the system role is not supported. User turns may include image-text or text-only inputs. To indicate that the input contains an image, add {"type": "image"} to the content part of the input and then pass the image data to the processor:

You can continue the conversation about the image. Remember, however, that if you provide a new image in a new user turn, the model will refer to the new image from that moment on. You can’t query about two different images at the same time. This is an example of the previous conversation continued, where we add the assistant turn to the conversation and ask for some more details:

You can also automatically quantize the model, loading it in 8-bit or even 4-bit mode with the bitsandbytes library. This is how you’d load the generation pipeline in 4-bit:

You can then apply the chat template, use the processor, and call the model just like you did before.

You can run both Llama 3.2 1B and 3B directly on your device's CPU/ GPU/ Browser using several open-source libraries like the following.

Llama.cpp is the go-to framework for all things cross-platform on-device ML inference. We provide quantized 4-bit & 8-bit weights for both 1B & 3B models in this collection. We expect the community to embrace these models and create additional quantizations and fine-tunes. You can find all the quantized Llama 3.2 models here.

Here’s how you can use these checkpoints directly with llama.cpp.

Install llama.cpp through brew (works on Mac and Linux).

You can use the CLI to run a single generation or invoke the llama.cpp server, which is compatible with the Open AI messages specification.

You’d run the CLI using a command like this:

You can also use llama-cpp-python to access these models programmatically in Python. Pip install the library from PyPI using:

You can even run Llama 3.2 in your browser (or any JavaScript runtime like Node.js, Deno, or Bun) using Transformers.js. You can find the ONNX model on the Hub. If you haven't already, you can install the library from NPM using:

MLC.ai Web-LLM is a high-performance in-browser LLM inference engine that brings language model inference directly onto web browsers with hardware acceleration. Everything runs inside the browser with no server support and is accelerated with WebGPU.

WebLLM is fully compatible with OpenAI API. That is, you can use the same OpenAI API on any open-source models locally, with functionalities including streaming, JSON-mode, function-calling, etc.

After successfully initializing the engine, you can now invoke chat completions using OpenAI style chat APIs through the engine.chat.completions interface.

TRL supports chatting and fine-tuning with the Llama 3.2 text models out of the box:

Support for fine tuning Llama 3.2 Vision is also available in TRL with this script.

You can also check out this notebook for LoRA fine-tuning using transformers and PEFT.

Releasing such models with support and evaluations in the ecosystem would not be possible without the contributions of thousands of community members who have contributed to transformers, text-generation-inference, vllm, pytorch, LM Eval Harness, and many other projects. Hat tip to the VLLM team for their help in testing and reporting issues. This release couldn't have happened without all the support of Clémentine, Alina, Elie, and Loubna for LLM evaluations, Nicolas Patry, Olivier Dehaene, and Daniël de Kok for Text Generation Inference; Lysandre, Arthur, Pavel, Edward Beeching, Amy, Benjamin, Joao, Pablo, Raushan Turganbay, Matthew Carrigan, and Joshua Lochner for transformers, transformers.js, TRL, and PEFT support; Nathan Sarrazin and Victor for making Llama 3.2 available in Hugging Chat; Brigitte Tousignant and Florent Daudens for communication; Julien, Simon, Pierric, Eliott, Lucain, Alvaro, Caleb, and Mishig from the Hub team for Hub development and features for launch.

And big thanks to the Meta Team for releasing Llama 3.2 and making it available to the open AI community!

#10881. Converting Vertex-Colored Meshes to Textured Meshes

Convert vertex-colored meshes to UV-mapped, textured meshes.

Vertex colors are a straightforward way to add color information directly to a mesh's vertices. This is often the way generative 3D models like InstantMesh produce meshes. However, most applications prefer UV-mapped, textured meshes.

This tutorial walks through a quick solution to convert vertex-colored meshes to UV-mapped, textured meshes. This includes The Short Version to get results quickly, and The Long Version for an in-depth walkthrough.

Install the InstantTexture library for easy conversion. This is a small library we wrote that implements the steps described in The Long Version below.

The code below converts a vertex-colored .obj mesh to a UV-mapped, textured .glb mesh and saves it to output.glb.

For a detailed walkthrough, continue reading.

Load the vertex-colored input mesh. This should be a .obj file located at input_mesh_path.

If it's a local file, use trimesh.load() instead of trimesh.load_remote().

If this fails, ensure the mesh is a valid .obj file with vertex colors.

This is the most time-consuming part of the process.

Remap the vertices and vertex colors to the uv map.

Construct a texture buffer that is upscaled by an upscale_factor to create a higher quality texture.

Fill in the texture of the UV-mapped mesh using barycentric interpolation.

Let's visualize how the texture looks so far.

As we can see, the texture has a lot of holes.

To correct for this, we'll combine 4 techniques:

As we can see, the texture is now much smoother and has no holes.

This can be further improved with more advanced techniques or manual texture editing.

Finally, we can construct a new mesh with the generated uv coordinates and texture.

Et voilà! The mesh is UV-mapped and textured.

To export it when running locally, call mesh.export("output.glb").

As you can see, the mesh still has many small artifacts.

The quality of the UV map and texture are also far below the standards of a production-ready mesh.

However, if you're looking for a quick solution to map from a vertex-colored mesh to a UV-mapped mesh, then this approach may be useful for you.

This tutorial walked through how to convert a vertex-colored mesh to a UV-mapped, textured mesh.

#10880. Top 5 AI Animation Generators in 2026: Features, Strengths, and Limits

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A few years ago, animating a ten-second scene meant storyboards, rigging and a lot of patience. Today you can type a sentence, upload a drawing or point at a reference clip and get moving footage back in a minute or two. The results are uneven, but they are good enough that designers, marketers and indie developers now use them for storyboards, product teasers, game trailers and social content.

The catch is that these tools are not interchangeable. Some excel at cinematic camera moves, some at editing footage you already have, and some at a particular visual style. This guide compares five AI animation generators, what each one is best at and where it falls short. Plans, credits and model names change quickly, so check each vendor's pricing page before you commit.

Runway is a cloud workspace for generating and editing video, images and audio in one place. Its current video model is Gen-4.5, which Runway promotes for motion quality, prompt adherence and visual fidelity. The platform also offers agent and workflow tools, mobile apps for iPhone and Android, and an API for developers.

Best for: Creators who want to generate a shot and then keep refining it in the same environment, and teams that need an API.

Limitations: There is a lot to learn, and credit costs add up when you iterate. Runway offers a free trial, but check the pricing page for current limits.

Kling AI is an AI video and image generator with a creative studio for image generation, video generation and motion control. It also includes an agent for brainstorming and scripting, and a node-based canvas for working through scripts, storyboards, images and video with multiple rounds of editing. Kling lists advertising, film, music videos and e-commerce among its use cases, and offers an API platform and automation options for producing video at scale.

Best for: Marketers and studios that want to move from script to storyboard to footage in a single workspace.

Limitations: The feature set is broad, so newcomers may need time to find the right workflow. Free credits were not described on the pages I checked, so confirm what is available before relying on it.

Luma focuses on turning still images into video with camera motion. Its workspace can create transitions between frames, extend clips, transform footage into new styles, reframe aspect ratios and add voice, music, captions and lip sync. It runs Luma's own Ray models and also gives access to several third-party models, so you can compare results without switching platforms.

Best for: Designers and illustrators who already have key art, product shots or concept images and want to bring them to life.

Limitations: Paid plans start at around $30 a month at the time of writing, and generation credits can run out quickly if you test many variations.

Pika is a creative platform covering video, images and audio. Its Video Studio can produce anything from a short clip to a multi-shot video of around 30 seconds, and its toolkit includes Extend Video, Motion Transfer, Swap Anything and Color Grade. Character Studio lets you create reusable characters, and separate studios handle music, speech and sound effects. Pika also exposes several video models, including its own Pika 2.5 alongside third-party options.

Best for: Social content creators who want effects, sound and edits in one tool.

Limitations: With so many tools and models, results vary from one to the next. Check the current pricing page for credit details.

Pollo AI is a generator that leans into one look: anime. Its animation generator creates anime-style videos from a text prompt and lets you adjust the video content, output style and size. The page offers eleven Japanese animator-inspired style options, such as Hayao Miyazaki and Makoto Shinkai, and the platform also provides a separate tool that converts existing video into anime.

Best for: Creators who want a consistent anime look for shorts, fan projects, music visuals or social posts without learning a full editing suite.

Limitations: The generator page describes text prompts as its input and does not state clip length, resolution or credit details, so test a few generations and review the terms before planning a project around it. As with any style-focused tool, the look is distinctive, which is a strength for anime projects and a limit for anything else.

Start with the job rather than the brand. If you need to edit and refine footage, Runway is a natural fit. If you want a script-to-video pipeline, look at Kling. If you have strong still images, try Luma. If you want effects and sound for social posts, Pika covers a lot of ground. If anime is the goal, Pollo AI is built for it.

Run the same prompt through two or three tools before paying for anything. Differences in motion, faces and text rendering show up quickly, and they are often more important than the feature list.

AI animation tools have moved from novelty to practical production aid. None of them replaces a skilled animator, but each can speed up storyboards, concepts and short-form content when matched to the right job. Try a few with a real project, compare the output, and keep a human in charge of the final cut. If you want a quick way to experiment with anime styles, you can create anime clips from a prompt and see how the results compare with the other tools on this list.

Are AI animation generators free? Most offer a free trial or limited credits, with paid plans for more generations and higher quality. Terms change often, so read each pricing page.

Can I use AI-generated animation commercially? It depends on the provider's terms and your plan. Check the licensing section before publishing client work.

Do I need animation experience? No, but knowing basic shot composition helps you write better prompts and judge the results.

Which tool is best for beginners? Pick one with a simple prompt-first workflow, test the free tier and move to a more advanced tool as your needs grow.

To achieve this, we've sourced 50 tasks spanning 9 categories, with 90% of tasks having native, non-translated content.

In this blog, we introduce both the evaluation suite itself and the BenCzechMark leaderboard, featuring over 25 open-source models of various sizes!

Since we use different metrics for the tasks, simply averaging wouldn't work due to varying scales. Instead, we've introduced a novel way to determine a final score: we let the models fight!

For every task and metric, we compute a test for statistical significance at α=0.05. This means the probability that the performance of model A equals that of model B is estimated to be less than 0.05. We use the following tests, each with varying statistical power:

We then compute a model's duel win score (DWS) - the proportion of duels won against all other models on that task. Finally, we calculate aggregate scores as follows:

This yields an easy-to-understand model score: Macro-averaged model win-rate!

#10878. A Short Summary of Chinese AI Global Expansion

In the early 15th century, Zheng He (also known as Chong Ho), a Chinese mariner and explorer during the early Ming Dynasty, led seven major naval expeditions, known as the "Voyages to the Western Oceans". His journey traced a path that went through Southeast Asia, the Middle East and then reached out to Africa. It was a bold move by China to establish diplomatic and trade relations with foreign lands, while exploring overseas opportunities. The word “出海” (Chu Hai, sailing abroad) has since held a special meaning about going global.

600 years later, China is once again making its mark internationally, evolving from a global manufacturing hub to a leader in ICT, electric vehicles, and AI technologies. By 2024, Chinese companies have accelerated their overseas expansion, particularly in AI. A June report from Feifan Research shows that out of 1,500 active AI companies worldwide, 751 are based in China, with 103 already expanding internationally. Many see this as a sign of China’s growing strength in tech innovation. Others argue that as domestic markets become saturated and competition intensifies, expanding overseas may have become the only viable option for these companies.

The first companies that are grabbing the opportunities of going global are, not surprisingly, leading Chinese tech giants. The likes of Huawei, Tencent, and Alibaba have chosen to focus on cloud computing and AI infrastructure when expanding overseas. In March 2024, Tencent Cloud partnered with Etihad Etisalat (Mobily), a leading telecom company in Saudi Arabia. Together, they launched the "Go Saudi" program, which aims to transform the digital landscape of the Saudi Arabia Kingdom as part of its Vision 2030 strategy​. In May, Huawei launched Galaxy AI as part of a larger initiative to boost digital intelligence transformation in North Africa. An initiative which is part of Huawei's broader $430 million, five-year investment plan aimed at accelerating smart transformation across the region. That same month, Alibaba announced the construction of data centers in Korea, Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand, and Mexico, alongside the release of the international version of its large model service platform, “Model Studio”.

Notably, these tech giants have centered their overseas strategies on Southeast Asia and the Middle East, aligning with China’s Belt and Road Initiative and the Digital Silk Road policy. Amid rising geopolitical tensions, choosing regions where Chinese is commonly spoken, such as Southeast Asia, or emerging markets like the Middle East and long-time allies like Africa, seems a more strategic choice.

ByteDance, referred to as an "App factory", has chosen to focus on familiar Western Business-to-Customer markets, launching 11 overseas applications in just seven months. CapCut, launched in 2020, released its paid version CapCut Pro in 2022, then integrated AI features in the beginning of 2024 and becoming one of the world’s most popular apps, with over 300 million monthly active users. According to Sensor Tower, by July 2024, CapCut had generated $125 million in cumulative revenue from mobile applications.

Startups, despite being in the early stages of commercialization, are also eager to join the overseas expansion. The Chinese AI unicorn startups have a different strategy based on adopting a model + application approach. Facing high costs for training models, some have begun to shift focus from updating foundational models to more profitable application and scenario exploration. For startups reliant on funding, expanding overseas has become a necessity amid intense domestic competition. Many early-stage companies have chosen Western to-C markets, launching productivity, creative, and companion apps based on their respective models. For example, among the “Big Six” ( refers to the six most-watched Chinese AI startups: 01.AI, Baichuan AI, Zhipu, Moonshot AI, MiniMax, StepFun. However, the list often changes, some think DeepSeek AI and OpenBMB should be included.), apps “Talkie” from MiniMax and “PopAI” from 01.AI which has gained millions of users and achieved a level of profitability.

China has the world's largest number of internet users and a vast pool of technical developers, and no one wants to be left behind in the AI boom. As more companies flood the space, AI technology has developed rapidly, but the growth of applications and use cases has been slower. Both industry giants and startups face growth stagnation and profit pressure.

Between October 2023 and September 2024, China released 238 LLMs. After more than a year of fierce competition, they entered a phase of consolidation. The pressure built up in May 2024 during the first price war, triggered by DeepSeek, an AI startup, which introduced architectural innovations that significantly reduced model inference costs. Following the announcement, major players like ByteDance, Tencent, Baidu, and Alibaba swiftly followed with price reductions, even cutting prices to below cost margins. This fierce competition stems from minimal technical differentiation between models and slower-than-expected productization.

From the launch of ChatGPT to July 2024, 78,612 AI companies have either been dissolved or suspended (resource:TMTPOST). The competition is not only pushing out the players from the ring, survivors are also drilling down to the niche to differentiate from the others. For example, the industry-specific LLMs are gaining traction, with a significant push from the government. The March 5, 2024 “Government Work Report” delivered by the Chinese Premier minister emphasized the "AI+" strategy, driving AI’s penetration across industries. By July 2024, the number of AI models registered with the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) exceeded 197, nearly 70% were industry-specific LLMs, particularly in sectors like finance, healthcare, and education. The peace will not last long, AI's rapid integration into vertical industries is expected to become a key area of another round of competition in the coming months.

Under this circumstance, going abroad seems to be a way out.

March 5, 2024: The China National Information Security Standardization Technical Committee (TC260) released a technical document outlining basic safety requirements for generative AI services.

September 14, 2024: The Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) proposed new rules requiring AI-generated content to be labeled, ensuring users can easily tell if content is human or machine-made.

Regulations are indispensable for any new industry, however they also increase compliance costs for companies, especially for SMEs. Former Microsoft engineer Shao Meng commented, "Tighter regulations, especially for to-C teams, may push more companies to expand overseas, including their products and even their teams."

On top of the policy pressure, the investment environment is getting more and more rational over the last 6 months compared to the AI fever when ChatGPT was out. By mid-2024, Chinese AI startups raised approximately $4.4 billion across 372 funding rounds, a significant drop from the peak in 2021, when investments reached $24.9 billion.

Compared to the domestic market, one particular element in certain overseas markets is that the individual customers have a greater willingness to pay, thanks to the healthy business environment. By proposing groundbreaking AI solutions meeting the local needs, Chinese AI companies can quickly develop stable revenue streams. For instance, in Southeast Asia, innovative approaches like AI-powered digital human livestreaming are breaking into the e-commerce live-streaming sector.

As for enterprise or government clients, emerging markets like Southeast Asia, the Middle East, and Africa have become the primary choices for Chinese AI companies as mentioned above. These regions, still in the early stages of digital transformation, are jumping directly to the latest technologies . Compared to saturated Western markets, these areas have less competition, higher potential for growth, and lower entry barriers, where Chinese AI tech giants are expanding their market share by capitalizing on their technological strengths, cost-efficient structures, and government support.

Technical Localization: Despite the magic of AI, there is still no one size fits all solution. In emerging markets with weaker infrastructure, companies need to adjust their products to accommodate network conditions, data storage, and algorithm adaptability. Meanwhile, in developed markets, complying with industry standards such as data localization and ISO certifications etc.

Despite the fast growing AI innovation in China, Chinese AI companies have not yet gained enough awareness in overseas markets. Releasing open-source projects on the Hugging Face Hub become an effective way to build global visibility. Beyond raising awareness, these models have also contributed valuable AI resources and diverse multilingual solutions to the global community. For example, at least one model from China appears on Hugging Face’s trending model leaderboard almost every one to two weeks. These include Alibaba’s Qwen series, which has been a “long-running hit” on Hugging Face’s Open LLM leaderboard, considered today to be one of the best open LLM in the world which support over 29 different languages; DeepSeek coder is another one, that is highly praise by the open source community; and Zhipu AI’s also open sourced its GLM series and CogVideo.

Through open-source initiatives, these projects have gained considerable influence in the international open-source community, helping to enhance recognition, trust, and competitiveness for the Chinese projects in the global market.

An interesting point is that many Chinese companies, after expanding overseas, tend to adopt a new brand name or prefer to promote themselves using the name of their models or applications. “Chinese companies often create new brands for oversea products, even one per country, while Western companies prefer to use unified product names globally.” Engineer from Hugging Face Tiezhen Wang said. This approach helps them fit into local markets better and shields them from geopolitical pressure at the same time.

AI for Good is no doubt an important initiative to explore the potential of AI for a bigger purpose, which is an all inclusive statement without borders. In Beijing, the China ESG30 Forum released the "2024 China Enterprises Global Expansion Strategy Report." This report highlighted the importance of ESG and AI, as two pillars for Chinese companies to integrate into a new phase of globalization. Some tech giants have already begun adopting green energy to drive the sustainable development of their global data centers, or using AI image recognition technologies to monitor wildlife, among others. AI applications are also being used with AI startups and traditional industries to co-develop green technologies, such as renewable energy and electric vehicles. Such innovations further promote product sustainability, helping Chinese firms stand out in the competitive landscape.

Chinese AI companies are at a critical turning point. Expanding overseas is not just a simple market expansion strategy but a necessary choice, because of a harsh domestic environment but also for seemingly promising overseas opportunities. However, overseas expansion is not guaranteed to succeed. Under unfamiliar markets and audiences, to be able to quickly adjust to the local market, comply with regulations and build awareness seems also no less challenging.

What’s more, AI is still in an early stage of development, and its true power is unleashed when AI companies find the sweet spot of being an AI enabler to reshape the industries. Going abroad is relevant today for Chinese AI companies to grow, but it would become even more relevant when it actually integrates and brings value to the local industries.

Zheng He’s expedition to the “west ocean” was powered by a whole nation strategy thanks to its strong economic power. History seems to be repeating itself today but with a different context: technological innovation thrives not through centralized national efforts, but through the dynamic forces of the free market, where competition, entrepreneurship, and open exchange drive creativity and progress. China’s AI companies have made a long way to rise, and they still are a long way to flourish.

Thanks to Tiezhen Wang, Luke Cheng, Shao Meng and Sam Guo for providing valuable feedback.

#10877. Introducing the Open FinLLM Leaderboard

Finding the best LLM models for finance use cases

The growing complexity of financial language models (LLMs) necessitates evaluations that go beyond general NLP benchmarks. While traditional leaderboards focus on broader NLP tasks like translation or summarization, they often fall short in addressing the specific needs of the finance industry. Financial tasks, such as predicting stock movements, assessing credit risks, and extracting information from financial reports, present unique challenges that require models with specialized skills. This is why we decided to create the Open FinLLM Leaderboard.

The leaderboard provides a specialized evaluation framework tailored specifically to the financial sector. We hope it fills this critical gap, by providing a transparent framework that assesses model readiness for real-world use with a one-stop solution. The leaderboard is designed to highlight a model's financial skill by focusing on tasks that matter most to finance professionals—such as information extraction from financial documents, market sentiment analysis, and forecasting financial trends.

The Open Financial LLM Leaderboard (OFLL) evaluates financial language models across a diverse set of categories that reflect the complex needs of the finance industry. Each category targets specific capabilities, ensuring a comprehensive assessment of model performance in tasks directly relevant to finance.

The selection of task categories in OFLL is intentionally designed to capture the full range of capabilities required by financial models. This approach is influenced by both the diverse nature of financial applications and the complexity of the tasks involved in financial language processing.

We use 40 tasks on this leaderboard, across these categories:

**FPB (Financial PhraseBank Sentiment Classification) **Description: Sentiment analysis of phrases in financial news and reports, classifying into positive, negative, or neutral categories.Metrics: Accuracy, F1-Score

FiQA-SA (Sentiment Analysis in Financial Domain)Description: Sentiment analysis in financial media (news, social media). Classifies sentiments into positive, negative, and neutral, aiding in market sentiment interpretation.Metrics: F1-Score

TSA (Sentiment Analysis on Social Media)Description: Sentiment classification for financial tweets, reflecting public opinion on market trends. Challenges include informal language and brevity. Metrics: F1-Score, RMSE

Headlines (News Headline Classification)Description: Classification of financial news headlines into sentiment or event categories. Critical for understanding market-moving information.Metrics: AvgF1

FOMC (Hawkish-Dovish Classification)Description: Classification of FOMC statements as hawkish (favoring higher interest rates) or dovish (favoring lower rates), key for monetary policy predictions.Metrics: F1-Score, Accuracy

FinArg-ACC (Argument Unit Classification)Description: Identifies key argument units (claims, evidence) in financial texts, crucial for automated document analysis and transparency.Metrics: F1-Score, Accuracy

FinArg-ARC (Argument Relation Classification)Description: Classification of relationships between argument units (support, opposition) in financial documents, helping analysts construct coherent narratives.Metrics: F1-Score, Accuracy

MultiFin (Multi-Class Sentiment Analysis)Description: Classification of diverse financial texts into sentiment categories (bullish, bearish, neutral), valuable for sentiment-driven trading.Metrics: F1-Score, Accuracy

MA (Deal Completeness Classification)Description: Classifies mergers and acquisitions reports as completed, pending, or terminated. Critical for investment and strategy decisions.Metrics: F1-Score, Accuracy

MLESG (ESG Issue Identification)Description: Identifies Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) issues in financial documents, important for responsible investing.Metrics: F1-Score, Accuracy

NER (Named Entity Recognition in Financial Texts)Description: Identifies and categorizes entities (companies, instruments) in financial documents, essential for information extraction.Metrics: Entity F1-Score

FINER-ORD (Ordinal Classification in Financial NER)Description: Extends NER by classifying entity relevance within financial documents, helping prioritize key information.Metrics: Entity F1-Score

FinRED (Financial Relation Extraction)Description: Extracts relationships (ownership, acquisition) between entities in financial texts, supporting knowledge graph construction.Metrics: F1-Score, Entity F1-Score

SC (Causal Classification)Description: Classifies causal relationships in financial texts (e.g., "X caused Y"), aiding in market risk assessments.Metrics: F1-Score, Entity F1-Score

CD (Causal Detection)Description: Detects causal relationships in financial texts, helping in risk analysis and investment strategies.Metrics: F1-Score, Entity F1-Score

FinQA (Numerical Question Answering in Finance)Description: Answers numerical questions from financial documents (e.g., balance sheets), crucial for automated reporting and analysis.Metrics: Exact Match Accuracy (EmAcc)

TATQA (Table-Based Question Answering)Description: Extracts information from financial tables (balance sheets, income statements) to answer queries requiring numerical reasoning.Metrics: F1-Score, EmAcc

ConvFinQA (Multi-Turn QA in Finance)Description: Handles multi-turn dialogues in financial question answering, maintaining context throughout the conversation.Metrics: EmAcc

FNXL (Numeric Labeling)Description: Labels numeric values in financial documents (e.g., revenue, expenses), aiding in financial data extraction.Metrics: F1-Score, EmAcc

FSRL (Financial Statement Relation Linking)Description: Links related information across financial statements (e.g., revenue in income statements and cash flow data).Metrics: F1-Score, EmAcc

EDTSUM (Extractive Document Summarization)Description: Summarizes long financial documents, extracting key information for decision-making.Metrics: ROUGE, BERTScore, BARTScore

ECTSUM (Extractive Content Summarization)Description: Summarizes financial content, extracting key sentences or phrases from large texts.Metrics: ROUGE, BERTScore, BARTScore

BigData22 (Stock Movement Prediction)Description: Predicts stock price movements based on financial news, using textual data to forecast market trends.Metrics: Accuracy, MCC

ACL18 (Financial News-Based Stock Prediction)Description: Predicts stock price movements from news articles, interpreting sentiment and events for short-term forecasts.Metrics: Accuracy, MCC

CIKM18 (Financial Market Prediction Using News)Description: Predicts broader market movements (indices) from financial news, synthesizing information for market trend forecasts.Metrics: Accuracy, MCC

#10876. A 10-Point Checklist for Legacy Application Modernization

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Legacy applications often support critical business operations, but keeping them running can become increasingly difficult. Outdated infrastructure, growing technical debt, security vulnerabilities, and limited integration capabilities can make these systems expensive to maintain and harder to adapt to changing business needs.

Modernizing them involves more than upgrading technology. You need to understand what the existing application does, identify which components need improvement, and manage the transition without disrupting essential operations.

This 10-point legacy application modernization checklist walks you through the process, from assessing your existing systems and selecting a modernization strategy to migrating data, testing applications, and measuring results.

Legacy application modernization is the process of updating existing software applications, their architecture, infrastructure, or underlying technologies to meet current business and technical requirements.

Depending on the application's condition, modernization may involve moving it to a new platform, improving its code, redesigning its architecture, or replacing it with a new solution.

The goal is to improve performance, security, scalability, maintainability, and the application's ability to support future business requirements.

Modernization isn't necessarily the same as cloud migration. Moving an application from on-premises infrastructure to the cloud changes where it runs, but it may leave its underlying architecture and technical limitations unchanged.

An organization can modernize an application without moving it to the cloud or combine both approaches as part of a larger transformation.

Use this checklist to track the ten essential steps involved in modernizing legacy applications.

1. Define modernization goals: Identify business problems and establish measurable success criteria.

2. Assess existing applications: Review infrastructure, technical debt, code quality, and performance limitations.

3. Map application dependencies: Document critical workflows, integrations, and business rules.

4. Choose a modernization strategy: Select an approach based on business value, cost, complexity, and risk.

5. Develop a roadmap and budget: Prioritize activities, estimate costs, assign responsibilities, and establish milestones.

6. Plan architecture and security: Design the target environment and address security, compliance, and availability requirements.

7. Prepare data migration: Plan data transfer, integration changes, and validation procedures.

8. Modernize incrementally: Validate the approach with a pilot and implement changes in manageable phases.

9. Test and deploy: Verify functionality, performance, security, and data integrity before production rollout.

10. Monitor and optimize: Measure results, support users, and continuously improve the modernized application.

Let's examine what each step involves and how to determine whether you're ready to proceed.

Before selecting technologies or planning development work, identify what the modernization initiative needs to achieve.

Clear business objectives help prioritize investments, guide technical decisions, and establish whether the project delivers meaningful improvements.

Start by examining the problems affecting your application's performance, reliability, or business value.

For example, a legacy order management system might still process transactions reliably but require extensive manual work whenever the business adds a new sales channel.

In this situation, improving integration capabilities may be more valuable than replacing the entire application.

An application's age alone doesn't justify a major technology investment. Whether legacy modernization makes sense for your business depends on the problems the existing system creates, the cost of maintaining it, and whether smaller improvements could resolve those issues.

Once you've identified the problems, translate them into measurable objectives.

If slow performance is the primary concern, establish a target for response times or transaction processing speed. If maintenance expenses are rising, determine what reduction in operating costs would justify the investment.

Relevant key performance indicators (KPIs) may include:

These baseline measurements will help determine whether the changes deliver the expected results.

Completion check: You have a documented business case identifying the problems to address, expected outcomes, measurable KPIs, and stakeholders responsible for approving success.

A legacy application assessment provides a clear picture of your current technology environment.

Without this assessment, teams may underestimate project complexity, overlook critical components, or choose a modernization approach that doesn't address the application's actual limitations.

Begin by creating an inventory of your applications and their supporting technologies.

Document each application's purpose, business owner, primary users, operating environment, programming languages, frameworks, databases, and infrastructure requirements.

Also identify software versions, third-party dependencies, licensing restrictions, and components approaching or past their end-of-support dates.

If your organization operates several legacy applications, use a consistent assessment framework. This makes it easier to compare their business importance, technical condition, and modernization urgency.

Review the application's codebase to identify issues that make maintenance and development difficult.

Look for tightly coupled components, duplicated logic, outdated libraries, insufficient automated tests, and undocumented configurations.

Pay particular attention to areas where small modifications regularly cause unexpected problems elsewhere in the system.

For example, if payment processing, inventory management, and customer records share tightly connected code, modifying one function could require extensive testing across the entire application.

Your infrastructure assessment should also cover hardware limitations, database compatibility, backup capabilities, operating systems, and unsupported dependencies.

Analyze how the application performs during normal operations and periods of increased demand.

Review response times, database queries, resource utilization, transaction volumes, and recurring failures.

Existing monitoring data and incident records can reveal problems that aren't immediately visible during routine use.

Determine whether performance limitations originate from inefficient application code, infrastructure capacity, database design, or external dependencies.

This distinction matters because adding computing resources won't necessarily resolve problems caused by poor application logic.

Completion check: You have an application inventory and technical assessment report documenting major components, technical debt, operational risks, and performance limitations.

Legacy applications rarely operate independently. They exchange data with other systems, support interconnected business processes, and often contain business rules that aren't fully documented.

Understanding these dependencies is essential because changing one component can affect several other applications or workflows.

Document the processes that rely on the application, including the steps users follow, the data they need, and the expected outcomes.

Work with business users, application owners, operations teams, and developers familiar with the system.

Identify processes that cannot tolerate significant interruption, such as payment processing, order fulfillment, customer authentication, or financial reporting.

Don't overlook activities that happen less frequently. Month-end financial reports, annual calculations, and scheduled data exchanges may depend on functionality that isn't exercised during everyday operations.

Map how the application communicates with databases, APIs, third-party services, and other internal systems.

Include scheduled jobs, file transfers, message queues, authentication services, and reporting tools.

Some legacy applications contain years of accumulated business logic.

Rules for pricing, approvals, calculations, or customer eligibility may exist only in source code, database procedures, or undocumented workflows.

Identify these rules before modifying the underlying implementation.

Where possible, create automated tests that capture existing expected behavior. These tests can help verify that the modernized application preserves required functionality.

Completion check: Critical workflows, system dependencies, integrations, and business rules are documented and reviewed by the relevant business and technical owners.

The appropriate modernization strategy depends on the application's technical condition, business importance, budget, and future requirements.

Not every application needs to be rebuilt. Some systems require targeted improvements, while others may be better replaced or retired.

Common legacy application modernization strategies include:

Different applications within the same organization may require different approaches.

Evaluate each option against your technical constraints and business requirements.

Consider implementation effort, expected benefits, ongoing maintenance costs, required expertise, and potential disruption.

For example, replatforming may be suitable for an application that operates reliably but depends on aging infrastructure. Rearchitecting may be necessary when tightly coupled components prevent independent updates or scaling.

A complete rebuild requires particular caution. Recreating undocumented functionality can be expensive, and important business rules may be lost if the existing system hasn't been thoroughly assessed.

The right strategy should solve the identified problems without introducing unnecessary cost or complexity.

Completion check: Each application has a selected modernization strategy, documented rationale, estimated effort, and an approved decision on whether to modernize, retain, replace, or retire it.

Once you've selected a modernization approach, convert it into an actionable plan.

Your roadmap should establish what will change, in what order, who will be responsible, and how progress will be evaluated.

Prioritize modernization work according to business value, technical complexity, urgency, and dependencies.

Applications with unsupported components or significant security risks may require early attention. However, starting with the most complex application isn't always the best choice.

A smaller, lower-risk application can provide an opportunity to validate tools, workflows, and team capabilities before modernizing more critical systems.

Dependencies also affect the sequence. For example, a shared authentication service may need to be updated before applications that rely on it can be migrated.

Prepare a budget covering the full modernization process rather than development alone.

Compare upfront implementation expenses with expected operating costs over time.

A modernization approach with a lower initial cost may still require significant ongoing maintenance.

Allow contingency for unexpected issues, particularly when legacy documentation is incomplete or system dependencies remain uncertain.

Divide the project into phases with defined deliverables and approval requirements.

Assign responsible owners for architecture, development, security, data migration, testing, and business acceptance.

Establish how project risks will be reported and who can approve changes to scope, budget, or deployment schedules.

Keep the roadmap adaptable. Findings from pilot implementations or migration rehearsals may require changes to the original plan.

Completion check: Your modernization roadmap includes prioritized activities, estimated costs, responsible owners, dependencies, milestones, and approval checkpoints.

The target architecture determines how the modernized application will operate, scale, integrate with other systems, and remain maintainable.

Security and compliance requirements should be incorporated into the design from the beginning.

Choose an architecture that fits the application's actual requirements.

Possible approaches include a modular monolith, service-oriented architecture, microservices, or event-driven components.

Microservices aren't automatically the best option. Although they allow independent deployment and scaling of components, they also introduce complexity in communication, monitoring, deployment, and data management.

For smaller applications or tightly integrated business processes, a well-structured modular architecture may be easier to maintain.

Document architectural decisions covering application components, data storage, interfaces, infrastructure requirements, and operational responsibilities.

Identify security weaknesses that should be resolved during modernization.

Review authentication, authorization, encryption, secrets management, logging, and access to sensitive information.

Evaluate third-party dependencies and establish processes for vulnerability scanning, patching, and security testing.

Regulatory and contractual requirements should also influence the target design.

Security controls should be applied throughout development and deployment rather than added shortly before release.

Define how the application will remain available and recover from failures.

Establish recovery time objectives (RTOs) and recovery point objectives (RPOs) based on business requirements.

Plan backup procedures, restoration testing, appropriate redundancy, and monitoring for critical components.

Validate that the target environment can support the required availability and recovery objectives.

Completion check: The target architecture has documented design decisions, security controls, compliance requirements, availability objectives, and recovery procedures.

Data migration is one of the most sensitive stages of legacy application modernization.

Legacy databases may contain inconsistent records, outdated formats, duplicated information, or relationships that newer systems handle differently.

A migration strategy needs to explain how data will be transferred, validated, and made available without compromising business operations.

Begin by reviewing the quality and structure of existing data.

Identify missing values, duplicate records, inconsistent formats, obsolete fields, and relationships that could create migration problems.

Document how existing data structures correspond to the target system.

For example, a legacy customer database might store contact details in a single field, while the new application requires separate fields for email addresses and phone numbers.

The migration process needs defined transformation rules to handle these differences.

Determine which records must be migrated, archived, retained for compliance, or excluded.

Choose a migration approach based on data volume, application availability requirements, and acceptable downtime.

Depending on the system, this may involve a scheduled migration during a maintenance window, staged transfers, or synchronization between old and new environments.

Identify integrations that will need modification.

Where applications exchange information through APIs, files, or messaging systems, verify that the modernized implementation supports the required data formats and business behavior.

If the legacy and modernized applications will operate simultaneously, define how data updates will be synchronized between them.

Test the migration process using representative datasets before transferring production data.

Validate record counts, field values, relationships, and critical business calculations.

For sensitive or business-critical information, use appropriate reconciliation methods, including integrity checks where applicable.

Document how inconsistencies will be identified and resolved.

Also establish what happens if migration fails or the application needs to return to its previous environment.

Completion check: Data mapping rules are approved, migration rehearsals have been completed, and reconciliation procedures can verify data accuracy.

Modernizing an entire application in a single major release can increase project risk, particularly when the system supports critical business operations.

An incremental approach allows teams to validate decisions, identify problems earlier, and limit the impact of failures.

Select a manageable component or workload to validate your modernization approach.

The pilot should test an important assumption, such as whether the target platform supports the application, whether a legacy integration can be replaced, or whether an architectural change improves performance.

Define success criteria before implementation.

A useful pilot should provide evidence that the approach is technically feasible and that the team can manage its operational requirements.

Use the findings to improve estimates, identify missing skills, and refine the broader implementation plan.

Divide the application into manageable migration or development units where its architecture allows.

One approach is the Strangler Fig pattern, which gradually replaces legacy functionality while the remaining parts of the original application continue operating.

For example, an organization might modernize customer notifications first, followed by reporting and then core transaction processing.

This can reduce the risks associated with replacing an entire system at once.

However, incremental modernization also requires careful coordination. Temporary integrations, duplicated components, and parallel systems can introduce complexity.

Each phase should have defined boundaries, validation requirements, and completion criteria.

Establish repeatable processes for developing, testing, and deploying application changes.

Continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines can automate builds, execute tests, and promote approved changes through environments.

Use version control, consistent configuration management, and infrastructure as code where appropriate.

Include security and quality checks in the delivery process to reduce the risk of introducing defects during frequent releases.

Completion check: The pilot has validated the selected approach, implementation is divided into manageable phases, and repeatable build, test, and deployment processes are established.

Modernization isn't complete when the new application runs successfully in a development environment.

It must perform the required business functions, communicate correctly with connected systems, and meet operational expectations before production rollout.

Develop a testing plan based on the application's critical workflows and identified risks.

Automate repeatable tests where practical, especially for critical business processes.

Compare results against the performance baselines and acceptance criteria established earlier.

Business users should verify that the modernized application supports their actual workflows.

User acceptance testing (UAT) should include routine operations, exception handling, reporting requirements, and tasks that depend on specialized business knowledge.

Use representative migrated data during testing.

Confirm that critical records, calculations, and reports remain accurate after the transition.

Resolve issues affecting essential operations before approving production deployment.

Prepare a documented deployment plan outlining the sequence of activities, responsible teams, communication channels, and expected service interruptions.

Choose a deployment method appropriate for the application, such as a phased rollout, canary release, or scheduled cutover.

Establish measurable conditions that would stop deployment or trigger a rollback.

Rollback planning must account for data changes made after cutover. Restoring an earlier application version doesn't automatically restore database consistency, especially if new transactions have already been processed.

Rehearse deployment and recovery procedures in a suitable non-production environment.

Completion check: Required tests have passed, business owners have approved acceptance criteria, and deployment, cutover, and recovery procedures have been validated.

The initial deployment marks the beginning of ongoing operation rather than the end of modernization.

The application needs continued monitoring and maintenance to ensure that expected improvements are sustained.

Compare post-modernization results against the baseline established at the beginning of the project.

Track metrics linked to your business objectives, such as application availability, maintenance costs, response times, deployment frequency, security vulnerabilities, and user satisfaction.

Use monitoring tools, logs, traces, and alerts to identify problems that may not be visible through basic availability checks.

Review performance after deployment and at agreed intervals to determine whether the modernization initiative is meeting its objectives.

Technical improvements may introduce changes to established workflows.

Provide relevant training, updated documentation, and support resources for users and operational teams.

Ensure that administrators and developers understand the new architecture, deployment processes, monitoring tools, and incident response procedures.

Collect user feedback to identify usability issues or missing functionality.

Use production data and operational feedback to guide further improvements.

Optimization may involve updating dependencies, improving database queries, adjusting infrastructure capacity, strengthening security controls, or simplifying application components.

Once replacement functionality is stable and approved, begin decommissioning components that are no longer needed.

Before retirement, confirm that dependent applications have been migrated, necessary records are retained, and archival or compliance obligations have been met.

Removing unused infrastructure and software can reduce maintenance costs and unnecessary security exposure.

Completion check: Monitoring and support responsibilities are established, modernization KPIs are reviewed, and unused legacy components have an approved retirement plan.

Organizations without the internal resources to manage legacy modernization may need support from an external software development company.

Depending on the project, a development partner can assist with application assessments, code refactoring, architecture redesign, system integration, data migration, and implementation.

Companies offering custom software development and application modernization services include:

Idea Maker: Provides custom software development and legacy application modernization services, including application assessments, code refactoring, architecture redesign, and cloud migration.

ScienceSoft: Offers custom software development, legacy software modernization, application reengineering, cloud migration, and system integration services.

Itransition: Provides custom application development, legacy application modernization, system integration, software migration, and post-modernization support.

Simform: Offers digital product engineering, software modernization, cloud and platform engineering, and data integration services.

These are examples of providers rather than a ranked comparison.

When evaluating a development partner, consider their experience with your existing technology stack, ability to handle complex integrations, approach to data security, and experience delivering projects with similar requirements.

Ask prospective providers how they assess legacy systems, manage migration risks, preserve critical business logic, and validate application functionality before deployment.

The main steps are defining business goals, assessing existing applications, mapping dependencies, choosing a modernization strategy, developing a roadmap, designing the target architecture, planning data migration, implementing changes, testing and deploying, and continuously optimizing the application.

The exact sequence may vary depending on the application's complexity and business requirements.

Start by evaluating the application's business value, technical condition, dependencies, and future requirements.

Rehosting or replatforming may be sufficient when the application functions well and infrastructure is the primary concern.

Refactoring or rearchitecting may be necessary when code quality or architectural limitations affect maintainability and scalability.

Rebuilding or replacing becomes an option when the existing implementation no longer meets business needs or would be too costly to maintain.

Compare expected benefits, implementation costs, risks, and ongoing maintenance requirements before making a decision.

Common risks include undocumented dependencies, data loss or corruption, unexpected downtime, security vulnerabilities, integration failures, and loss of essential business functionality.

Projects may also experience delays or budget overruns when technical complexity is underestimated.

These risks can be reduced through early assessment, phased implementation, migration rehearsals, comprehensive testing, and validated recovery procedures.

The timeline depends on the application's size, architecture, technical debt, data complexity, integrations, and selected modernization approach.

A limited rehosting or refactoring project generally requires less effort than rebuilding a large application or modernizing several interconnected systems.

A reliable estimate requires an initial technical assessment. A pilot or proof of concept can help validate assumptions about implementation effort and potential challenges.

Measure success against the business and technical objectives established before implementation.

Relevant indicators include application performance, availability, maintenance costs, security improvements, deployment speed, and user satisfaction.

For example, if reducing maintenance effort was the primary goal, lower support costs and faster resolution of application issues may be more meaningful than infrastructure performance alone.

Modernization success should be evaluated over time rather than only immediately after deployment.

Legacy application modernization works best when it follows a structured plan based on business needs and the realities of existing technology.

The ten steps in this checklist cover the key decisions and activities involved, from assessing legacy systems and selecting a modernization strategy to migrating data, validating functionality, and maintaining the resulting application.

Careful dependency mapping, realistic planning, incremental implementation, and thorough testing help reduce risks throughout the transition.

Start by assessing your existing applications and defining what modernization needs to achieve. Those findings will help you identify which systems deserve attention, where to invest resources, and how to approach modernization without introducing unnecessary complexity.

#10875. Improving Parquet Dedupe on Hugging Face Hub

The Xet team at Hugging Face is working on improving the efficiency of the Hub's storage architecture to make it easier and quicker for users to store and update data and models. As Hugging Face hosts nearly 11PB of datasets with Parquet files alone accounting for over 2.2PB of that storage, optimizing Parquet storage is of pretty high priority.

Most Parquet files are bulk exports from various data analysis pipelines or databases, often appearing as full snapshots rather than incremental updates. Data deduplication becomes critical for efficiency when users want to update their datasets on a regular basis. Only by deduplicating can we store all versions as compactly as possible, without requiring everything to be uploaded again on every update. In an ideal case, we should be able to store every version of a growing dataset with only a little more space than the size of its largest version.

Our default storage algorithm uses byte-level Content-Defined Chunking (CDC), which generally dedupes well over insertions and deletions, but the Parquet layout brings some challenges. Here we run some experiments to see how some simple modifications behave on Parquet files, using a 2GB Parquet file with 1,092,000 rows from the FineWeb dataset and generating visualizations using our dedupe estimator.

Parquet tables work by splitting the table into row groups, each with a fixed number of rows (for instance 1000 rows). Each column within the row group is then compressed and stored:

Intuitively, this means that operations which do not mess with the row grouping, like modifications or appends, should dedupe pretty well. So let's test this out!

Here we append 10,000 new rows to the file and compare the results with the original version. Green represents all deduped blocks, red represents all new blocks, and shades in between show different levels of deduplication.

We can see that indeed we are able to dedupe nearly the entire file, but only with changes seen at the end of the file. The new file is 99.1% deduped, requiring only 20MB of additional storage. This matches our intuition pretty well.

Given the layout, we would expect that row modifications to be pretty isolated, but this is apparently not the case. Here we make a small modification to row 10000, and we see that while most of the file does dedupe, there are many small regularly spaced sections of new data!

A quick scan of the Parquet file format suggests that absolute file offsets are part of the Parquet column headers (see the structures ColumnChunk and ColumnMetaData)! This means that any modification is likely to rewrite all the Column headers. So while the data does dedupe well (it is mostly green), we get new bytes in every column header.

In this case, the new file is only 89% deduped, requiring 230MB of additional storage.

Here we delete a row from the middle of the file (note: insertion should have similar behavior). As this reorganizes the entire row group layout (each row group is 1000 rows), we see that while we dedupe the first half of the file, the remaining file has completely new blocks.

This is mostly because the Parquet format compresses each column aggressively. If we turn off compression we are able to dedupe more aggressively:

However the file sizes are nearly 2x larger if we store the data uncompressed.

Is it possible to have the benefit of dedupe and compression at the same time?

One potential solution is to use not only byte-level CDC, but also apply it at the row level: we split row groups not based on absolute count (1000 rows), but on a hash of a provided “Key” column. In other words, I split off a row group whenever the hash of the key column % [target row count] = 0, with some allowances for a minimum and a maximum row group size.

I hacked up a quick inefficient experimental demonstration here.

With this, we are able to efficiently dedupe across compressed Parquet files even as I delete a row. Here we clearly see a big red block representing the rewritten row group, followed by a small change for every column header.

Based on these experiments, we could consider improving Parquet file dedupe-ability in a couple of ways:

While we will continue exploring ways to improve Parquet storage performance (Ex: perhaps we could optionally rewrite Parquet files before uploading? Strip absolute file offsets on upload and restore on download?), we would love to work with the Apache Arrow project to see if there is interest in implementing some of these ideas in the Parquet / Arrow code base.

In the meantime, we are also exploring the behavior of our data dedupe process on other common filetypes. Please do try our dedupe estimator and tell us about your findings!
