#10874. Faster Assisted Generation with Dynamic Speculation

⭐ In this blog post, we’ll explore dynamic speculative decoding —a novel method developed by Intel labs and Hugging Face that accelerates text generation by up to 2.7x, depending on the task. This method is the default operational mode for assisted generation starting from Transformers🤗 release 4.45.0 ⭐

Speculative decoding is a popular technique to accelerate the inference of large language models, while preserving their accuracy. As shown in the figure below, speculative decoding works by splitting the generative process into two stages. In the first stage, a fast, but less accurate draft model (AKA assistant) autoregressively generates a sequence of tokens. In the second stage, a large, but more accurate target model conducts parallelized verification over the generated draft tokens. This process allows the target model to produce multiple tokens in a single forward pass and thus accelerate autoregressive decoding. The success of speculative decoding largely hinges on the speculation lookahead (SL), i.e. the number of tokens produced by the draft model in each iteration. In practice, the SL is either a static value or based on heuristics, neither of which is optimal for squeezing out maximium performance during inference.

Transformers🤗 offers two distinct methods to determine the schedule for adjusting the number of draft (assistant) tokens during inference. The straightforward method, based on Leviathan et al., uses a static value of the speculation lookahead and involves generating a constant number of candidate tokens at each speculative iteration. Alternatively, a heuristic-based approach adjusts the number of candidate tokens for the next iteration based on the acceptance rate of the current iteration. If all speculative tokens are correct, the number of candidate tokens increases; otherwise, it decreases.

We anticipate that an enhanced optimization strategy for managing the number of generated draft tokens could squeeze out further latency reductions. For testing this thesis we utilize an oracle that determines the optimal speculation lookahead value for each speculative iteration. The oracle employs the draft model to autoregressively generate tokens until a discrepancy arises between the predicted tokens of the draft and target models. This process is repeated for each speculative iteration, ultimately identifying the optimal (maximum) number of draft tokens accepted per iteration. The draft/target token mismatch is identified using the rejection sampling algorithm, introduced by Leviathan et al., with zero temperature. This oracle realizes the full potential of speculative decoding by generating the maximum number of valid draft tokens at each step and minimizing the number of calls to both the draft and target models.

The left figure below illustrates the oracle and static speculation lookahead values across the speculative iterations of a code generation example from the MBPP dataset. A high variance in oracle speculation lookahead values (orange bars) is observed. The static speculation lookahead (blue bars), where the number of generated draft tokens is fixed to 5, performs 38 target forward passes and 192 draft forward passes, whereas the oracle speculation lookahead, performs only 27 target forward passes and 129 draft forward passes - a significant reduction. The right figure shows the oracle and static speculation lookahead across the entire Alpaca dataset.

Oracle and static speculation lookahead (SL) values on one MBPP example.

Average oracle speculation lookahead for the entire Alpaca dataset.

Both figures demonstrate significant variability in oracle speculation lookahead values, suggesting that a static speculation lookahead may be suboptimal.

In order to get closer to the Oracle and gain extra speedup, we developed a straightforward method to dynamically adjust the speculation lookahead value at each iteration. After generating each draft token, we determine whether the draft model should continue generating the next token or switch to the target model for verification. This decision is based on the assistant model's confidence in its prediction, estimated by the softmax of the logits. If the assistant model's confidence in the current token prediction falls below a predefined threshold, referred to as the assistant_confidence_threshold, it halts the token generation process for that iteration, even if the maximum number of speculative tokens num_assistant_tokens has not been reached. Once halted, the draft tokens generated during the current iteration are sent to the target model for verification.

We benchmarked the dynamic approach against the heuristic approach across a range of tasks and model pairings. The dynamic approach showed better performance in all tests. Notably, using the dynamic approach with Llama3.2-1B as the assistant for Llama3.1-8B, we observe speedups of up to 1.52x, whereas the heuristic approach showed no significant speedups with the same setup. Another observation is that codegen-6B-mono yields slowdown using the heuristic approach, whereas the dynamic approach shows speedup.

The results in the table reflect greedy decoding (temperature = 0). Similar trends were observed when using sampling (temperature > 0).

Our benchmark is publicly available allowing everyone to evaluate further improvements: https://github.com/gante/huggingface-demos/tree/main/experiments/faster_generation

Dynamic speculation has been integrated into release 4.45.0 of the Hugging Face Transformers library and now serves as the default operation mode for assisted decoding. To use assisted generation with dynamic speculation, no code changes are required—just execute the code as you normally would:

The default dynamic speculation lookahead parameters reflect optimal values but can be adjusted to improve performance for specific model pairs or datasets by using the following code:

To revert to the heuristic or constant (as in Leviathan et al.) approaches, simply set num_assistant_tokens_schedule to 'heuristic' or 'constant', respectively, set assistant_confidence_threshold=0 and num_assistant_tokens=5 as follows:

We introduced a faster strategy for assisted generation called dynamic speculative decoding, which outperforms heuristics-based methods as well as drawing a constant number of candidate tokens.

In an upcoming blog post, we'll show a new method for assisted generation: combine any target model with any assistant model! This will open the door for accelerating countless models on the Hugging Face Hub that do not have small enough assistant variants. For example, Phi 3, Gemma 2, CodeLlama and many more will be eligible for speculative decoding. Stay tuned!

#10873. Pin vs Noon in 2026: Which AI Recruiter Fits Your Team?

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Buyers are moving from pilots to purchases: 52% of talent leaders told Korn Ferry they plan to add autonomous agents to their teams in 2026 (1,674 leaders, October 2025), and SHRM's 2026 research puts recruiting at 27% of organizations using AI, the most of any HR function. For a wider field, see our guide to the best AI recruiting agents.

Noon details come from Noon's own pages or a named third party, checked October 14, 2026.

Pin (pin.com) is an AI recruiting platform that assists recruiters by finding candidates across the 850M+ profiles Pin says it covers across North America and Europe, writing outreach from each person's profile signals and booking interviews. Candidate data comes from professional networks, GitHub, Stack Overflow, open-source contributions, patents, academic publications and the broader web. You search in plain language, paste a job description, upload ideal résumés or import a role from your ATS. Each ranked candidate has a fit score and an AI-written reason, and the model learns from your team's accept and reject feedback.

The Pin recruiting agent has two modes. In Assist you approve each step. In Autopilot it sources, screens and ranks, drafts outreach, sends the email steps, follows up on silence, schedules interviews and updates your ATS. LinkedIn and SMS steps arrive as tasks with an AI-drafted message, and you send them. Closing and offers stay human. The agent asks clarifying questions ("Is remote considered?"), shows every action in a feed and works 24/7 alongside your team. Josh Volinsky, Co-Founder of Synergy Search, says: "Pin makes sourcing candidates so natural and I love how you can just talk to it like it's a recruiter on your team and it goes hunting."

Noon (noon.ai) is an AI recruiting platform from Portal Inc. in New York whose agents source across the open web, run email and SMS outreach and book interviews. You start from a pasted job description or posting URL. Noon extracts the title, location and "non-negotiables," and its Autopilot sourcing agent keeps searching as new people enter the market. Candidates land in a ranked feed with reasoning, and thumbs-up and thumbs-down feedback calibrates the search per role.

Noon also extends further down the funnel. Its AI Interviewer runs voice screening calls, its Notetaker joins live interviews, and Inbound Screening ranks ATS applicants and flags suspected fraud. Those tools sit downstream of sourcing. Pin concentrates on the outbound workflow, from search through scheduling, and adds the team layer around it: a shared inbox, a dedupe layer so two recruiters never contact the same person, funnel dashboards and a multi-client CRM for agencies.

Pin gives you natural-language filters plus advanced filters you set yourself, and paid plans include unlimited searches.

Noon steers the search through criteria set per role. Its pages describe titles, locations, years of experience, target-company lists and must-haves, plus non-negotiables Noon says it never relaxes. You adjust by chat and feedback. We found no public description of an open-ended filter panel like Pin's, so ask for one in a demo if ad hoc searching matters.

On consistency, Pin returns a ranked shortlist with a reason for every candidate from the first search, then improves as your team accepts and rejects. Noon says its feedback loop calibrates the model per role, but it doesn't say how long that takes. Compare day one with day ten yourself (see the trial plan below).

Pin writes each message from the candidate's profile signals and calibrates to your writing voice. Its sequences run across email, LinkedIn and SMS: automated email steps plus AI-drafted LinkedIn and SMS tasks in the same sequence, which the recruiter sends. Sequences adapt per candidate, and any reply pauses the sequence. Free is email-only. Replies go to a shared team inbox, and a dedupe layer stops two recruiters contacting the same person.

Noon writes an intro for each candidate and drops it into sequence templates you control. Sequences run on email and SMS.

The practical difference is how contact data is packaged. Every Pin plan includes contact credits (5 a week on Free, 500 a month on Solo, 1,000 per user a month on Professional, unlimited on Business), and a personal email, work email or phone number uses 1 credit. Noon says contact enrichment is unlimited. Revealing email and phone for 300 candidates a month uses 600 of the 1,000 credits included with each Professional seat.

Pin's AI interview scheduling handles time zones, hiring panels and reschedules, and confirmations land in your ATS. Pin lists 120+ ATS integrations, including Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby, Bullhorn, iCIMS and Jobvite. ATS integration is an add-on on Solo and Professional and is included on Business. Teams without an ATS can track candidates in Pin's Kanban pipeline, a mini ATS from first touch to signed offer.

Noon's AI Coordinator answers candidate questions and books interviews through your Calendly availability, then handles reschedules. Its integrations page lists 40+ systems, including all six above plus Workday, SAP SuccessFactors, UKG, Loxo and Recruiterflow, and Noon says ATS sync is part of its plan. Several other Noon pages still say "20+," so confirm your ATS is live before you commit.

Pin publishes its pricing on its pricing page (checked October 14, 2026). Free is $0 (5 contact credits a week, 1 job, 1 agent, email-only sequences, 3 searches a day). Solo is $99 per user per month billed annually, for one seat, with 500 contact credits a month included. Professional is $135 per user per month billed annually or $179 month to month, with 2 agents and 1,000 contact credits per user each month, a shared inbox and 5 mailboxes per user. Business is custom, with unlimited seats, credits and agents and ATS integration included.

Noon sells one plan, quoted per team. Its pricing page lists unlimited sourcing, email enrichment, contacts, agents and seats, with no credits or per-seat fees. Its get-started page invites teams to create a free account, yet most "Start free" buttons open a demo-booking calendar, and Noon does not say what the free account includes.

Worked example: three recruiters on Pin Professional

With Noon, you won't know the number until after a sales call. Noon prices one flat plan per team and says adding seats doesn't change it, while Pin's cost is known before you talk to anyone and scales predictably per seat. Get Noon's quote in writing and compare it against these figures, keeping in mind that Noon's bundle includes screening and note-taking tools you may not need.

Noon also offers a 10x ROI guarantee on annual plans. According to Noon's guarantee terms (checked October 14, 2026), it values recruiter time at $60 an hour, relies on Noon's own measurement of time saved and requires minimum weekly use.

Pin is SOC 2 Type 2 audited by a third party, encrypts data at rest and in transit, and is GDPR and CCPA ready, with documents in its trust center at trust.pin.com. SSO/SAML and SCIM come with the Business plan.

Noon says it holds SOC 2 Type II and GDPR compliance, runs an annual third-party penetration test and supports SSO and SAML. According to its security page (updated September 3, 2026), Noon also offers data residency options for enterprise agreements and makes the SOC 2 report and pen-test summary available under NDA. The page does not mention CCPA.

Pin is built for agencies scaling outbound, and for recruiters and teams of any size that want a known price and hands-on control. It brings a multi-client recruiting CRM, per-seat pricing that scales predictably and a Business plan with unlimited seats. Pin assists recruiters rather than replacing them. Noon's homepage claims 40% faster time to hire, a vendor-reported figure.

Noon is good for teams with heavy inbound application volume that want voice screening and interview notes bundled with sourcing, and that are comfortable buying through a sales quote. The caveats are an unpublished price and free-account details, and only three reviews on Trustpilot.

When Pin is not the right fit: teams that only need high-volume inbound applicant screening.

When Noon is a harder fit: buyers who need a price before a sales call, teams that want a free plan with published details, and anyone who wants independent reviews to check (three on Trustpilot, no G2 listing found).

Choose Pin if you: - want a published price and a free plan with no credit card - want to start in Assist mode and hand steps to Autopilot as you build trust - run a team where several recruiters share candidates and need dedupe and a shared inbox - run an agency and need pipelines per client

Choose Noon if you: - want one quoted plan that Noon says does not change with seats or lookups - need voice screening, a notetaker, inbound screening or fraud detection in the same product - are comfortable buying through a demo and a custom quote

Replacing LinkedIn Recruiter? See our LinkedIn Recruiter alternatives. Pin's Noon AI alternatives roundup covers seven more tools.

Pin's Free plan is email-only, so run the full email, LinkedIn and SMS task flow on a paid plan; Professional is available month to month at $179 per user.

For recruiters, agencies and outbound recruiting teams, Pin is the better choice: published pricing, a free plan, Assist and Autopilot modes, a shared inbox with dedupe, and a multi-client CRM for agencies. Noon fits teams that need voice screening and inbound fraud checks bundled with sourcing, though it publishes no price. Pin's Pin vs Noon breakdown covers the matchup in more detail.

Noon does not publish a price. It sells one plan with unlimited seats, contacts and agents, quoted per team after a demo. Pin lists prices openly: Free, Solo at $99 per month billed annually, and Professional at $135 per user per month billed annually ($179 month to month). Three recruiters on Pin Professional cost $4,860 a year on annual billing.

Not clearly. Noon's get-started page offers a free account, but most "Start free" buttons open a demo-booking calendar and Noon does not publish what the account includes. Pin's Free plan is public: 5 contact credits a week, 1 job, 1 agent, email-only sequences and 3 searches a day, with no credit card.

For recruiters and teams that want published pricing and a free start, Pin (pin.com) is the Noon AI alternative built for exactly that. Pin says it searches 850M+ profiles, offers Assist and Autopilot modes and integrates with 120+ ATS platforms. For the full field, see the best AI recruiting agents.

Noon is an operating product with a weekly changelog, but independent review volume is small: Trustpilot showed three positive reviews in October 2026, and we found no G2 listing. That is too few to judge, so run a trial and ask for references. Pin has 4.8/5 on G2 across 27 verified reviews, per pin.com. For more on Noon's review record, see Pin's Noon AI reviews guide.

For recruiters and agencies that want a known price and control over how much the agent does, Pin is the better fit, starting with a free plan. Noon is worth a demo if inbound volume is your main problem and you want voice screening and fraud checks bundled in; get its price in writing first. Test both on live roles before you decide.

Try Pin free at pin.com - no credit card required.

#10872. Scaling AI-based Data Processing with Hugging Face + Dask

The Hugging Face platform has many datasets and pre-trained models that make using and training state-of-the-art machine learning models increasingly accessible. However, it can be hard to scale AI tasks because AI datasets are often large (100s GBs to TBs) and using Hugging Face transformers for model inference can sometimes be computationally expensive.

Dask, a Python library for distributed computing, can handle out-of-core computing (processing data that doesn’t fit in memory) by breaking datasets into manageable chunks. This makes it easy to do things like:

In this post we show an example of data processing from the FineWeb dataset, using the FineWeb-Edu classifier to identify web pages with high educational value. We’ll show:

The FineWeb dataset consists of 15 trillion tokens of English web data from Common Crawl, a non-profit that hosts a public web crawl dataset updated monthly. This dataset is often used for a variety of tasks such as large language model training, classification, content filtering, and information retrieval across a variety of sectors.

It can take > 1 minute to download and read in a single file with pandas on a laptop.

Next, we’ll use the HF FineWeb-Edu classifier to judge the educational value of the web pages in our dataset. Web pages are ranked on a scale from 0 to 5, with 0 being not educational and 5 being highly educational. We can use pandas to do this on a smaller, 100-row subset of the data, which takes ~10 seconds on a M1 Mac with a GPU.

Note that we also added a step to check the available hardware inside the compute_scores function, because it will be distributed when we scale with Dask in the next step. This makes it easy to go from testing locally on a single machine (either on a CPU or maybe you have a MacBook with an Apple silicon GPU) to distributing across multiple machines (like NVIDIA GPUs).

The entire 2024 February/March crawl is 432 GB on disk, or ~715 GB in memory, split up across 250 Parquet files. Even on a machine with enough memory for the whole dataset, this would be prohibitively slow to do serially.

To scale up, we can use Dask DataFrame, which helps you process large tabular data by parallelizing pandas. It closely resembles the pandas API, making it easy to go from testing on a single dataset to scaling out to the full dataset. Dask works well with Parquet, the default format on Hugging Face datasets, to enable rich data types, efficient columnar filtering, and compression.

We’ll apply the compute_scores function for text classification in parallel on our Dask DataFrame using map_partitions, which applies our function in parallel on each pandas DataFrame in the larger Dask DataFrame. The meta argument is specific to Dask, and indicates the data structure (column names and data types) of the output.

Note that we’ve picked a batch_size that works well for this example, but you’ll likely want to customize this depending on the hardware, data, and model you’re using in your own workflows (see the HF docs on pipeline batching).

Now that we’ve identified the rows of the dataset we’re interested in, we can save the result for other downstream analyses. Dask DataFrame automatically supports distributed writing to Parquet. Hugging Face uses commits to track dataset changes and allows writing a Dask DataFrame in parallel.

Since this creates one commit per file, it is recommended to squash the history after the upload:

Alternatively you can use this custom function which uploads multiple files per commit.

There are a number of ways to deploy Dask on a variety of hardware. Here, we’ll use Coiled to deploy Dask on the cloud so we can spin up VMs as needed, and then clean them up when we’re done.

The workflow took ~5 hours to complete and we had good GPU hardware utilization.

Putting it all together, here is the complete workflow:

Hugging Face + Dask is a powerful combination. In this example, we scaled up our classification task from 100 rows to 211 million rows by using Dask + Coiled to run the workflow in parallel across multiple GPUs on the cloud.

This same type of workflow can be used for other use cases like:

Reliability is everything, especially when you spend real time and money on gaming. I’ve been impressed by how consistent this venue is: https://btvs1.com/ For anyone who wants a stable, well-organized gaming environment across the territory of India, it delivers exactly what most players expect and more, without unnecessary complications.

#10871. Welcome, Gradio 5

We’ve been hard at work over the past few months, and we are excited to now announce the stable release of Gradio 5.

With Gradio 5, developers can build production-ready machine learning web applications that are performant, scalable, beautifully designed, accessible, and follow best web security practices, all in a few lines of Python.

To give Gradio 5 a spin, simply type in your terminal:

and start building your first Gradio application.

If you have used Gradio before, you might be wondering what’s different about Gradio 5.

Our goal with Gradio 5 was to listen to and address the most common pain points that we’ve heard from Gradio developers about building production-ready Gradio apps. For example, we’ve heard some developers tell us:

"This Gradio app looks old-school" → Many of the core Gradio components, including Buttons, Tabs, Sliders, as well as the high-level chatbot interface, have been refreshed with a more modern design in Gradio 5. We’re also releasing a new set of built-in themes, to let you easily create fresh-looking Gradio apps 🎨

“I can’t build realtime apps in Gradio” → We have unlocked low-latency streaming in Gradio! We use base64 encoding and websockets automatically where it offers speedups, support WebRTC via custom components, and have also added significantly more documentation and example demos that are focused on common streaming use cases, such as webcam-based object detection, video streaming, real-time speech transcription and generation, and conversational chatbots. 🎤

"LLMs don't know Gradio" → Gradio 5 ships with an experimental AI Playground where you can use AI to generate or modify Gradio apps and preview the app right in your browser immediately: https://www.gradio.app/playground

Gradio 5 provides all these features while maintaining Gradio’s simple and intuitive developer-facing API. Since Gradio 5 intended to be a production-ready web framework for all kinds of machine learning applications, we've also made significant improvements around web security (including getting a 3rd-party audit of Gradio) -- more about that in an upcoming post!

Gradio apps that did not raise any deprecation warnings in Gradio 4.x should continue to work in Gradio 5, with a small number of exceptions. See a list of breaking changes in Gradio 5 here.

Many of the changes we’ve made in Gradio 5 are designed to enable new functionality that we will be shipping in the coming weeks. Stay tuned for:

Multi-page Gradio apps, along with native navbars and sidebars

Support for running Gradio apps on mobile using PWA and potentially native app support

More media components to support emerging modalities around images and videos

A richer DataFrame component with support for common spreadsheet-type operations

One-line integrations with machine learning model and API providers

Further improvements that will decrease the memory consumption of Gradio apps

And much more! With Gradio 5 providing a robust foundation to build web applications, we’re excited to really get started letting developers build all sorts of ML apps with Gradio.

#10870. A Security Review of Gradio 5

We audited Gradio 5 so that your machine learning apps are safe!

In the past few years, Gradio (>6 million monthly Pypi installs) has become the default way to build machine learning web applications in Python. In just a few lines of code, you can create a user interface for an image generation app, a chatbot, or any other kind of ML app and share it with others using Gradio’s built-in share links or Hugging Face Spaces.

Our goal with Gradio is to allow developers to build web applications that work great out-of-the-box for machine learning use cases. This has meant letting you, as a developer, easily build applications that:

...even if you are not an expert in scaling, accessibility, or UI/UX!

Now, we’re adding web security to this list. We asked Trail of Bits, a well-known cybersecurity company, to conduct an independent audit of Gradio. The security issues they discovered were all fixed ahead of the Gradio 5 release.

This means that machine learning apps that you build with Gradio 5 will follow best practices when it comes to web security without any significant changes to your code.

In the past couple of years, the Gradio team has worked with the community to patch security vulnerabilities as they are discovered. But as Gradio’s popularity has grown (with >470,000 Gradio apps currently on Hugging Face Spaces), ensuring security has become even more important.

So in Gradio 5, we decided to take a different approach -- do a preemptive security audit of the Gradio codebase so that your machine learning applications built with Gradio 5 are safe by default.

We asked Trail of Bits to conduct an independent and comprehensive audit of Gradio. Their team of experts in AI and Application Security identified security risks in the Gradio codebase in 4 general scenarios:

Then, we worked closely with Trail of Bits to identify mitigation strategies for each of these risks. Gradio’s simplicity and ease of use, while beneficial for developers, also presented unique security challenges, as we didn’t want developers to need to set up complex security measures like CORS and CSP policies.

By the end of the collaboration, we fixed all of the security risks that were identified by Trail of Bits. All the fixes were validated by Trail of Bits, and are included in the Gradio 5.0 release. While it is impossible to prove the absence of security vulnerabilities, this is a major step in giving reassurance that your Gradio apps are safe.

We outline below the major security vulnerabilities that were discovered by Trail of Bits corresponding to the 4 scenarios above. In the interest of transparency and the spirit of open-source, we are making the full security report public, and more details for each of these issues can be found in the report.

Gradio apps deployed on Hugging Face Spaces or other servers

TOB-GRADIO-3: A full read GET-based SSRF that would allow attackers to make requests to and read the responses from arbitrary endpoints, including those on the user’s internal network.

TOB-GRADIO-10: Arbitrary file type uploads that would allow an attacker to host XSS payloads on a user’s Gradio server. In the context of an authenticated Gradio server, an attacker could use this to take over user accounts when the victim accesses an attacker’s malicious website.

TOB-GRADIO-13: A race condition that allows an attacker to reroute user traffic to their server and steal uploaded files or chatbot conversations.

TOB-GRADIO-16: Several components’ post-process functions could allow attackers to leak arbitrary files in very simple Gradio server configurations.

Gradio apps shared with built-in share links

TOB-GRADIO-19: Remote code execution (RCE) with the root user on the Gradio API Server via a nginx misconfiguration that exposed the unauthenticated docker API. This allowed an attacker to provide a malicious host and port in step 2 of the diagram and redirect all frp tunnels to a malicious server that records all user traffic, including uploaded files and chatbox conversations.

TOB-GRADIO-11: Lack of robust encryption in communications between the frp-client and frp-server, allowing attackers in a position to intercept requests (the ones from steps 6 and 7 in the diagram above) to read and modify the data going to and from the frp-server.

Supply chain vulnerabilities originating from the Gradio CI pipeline

TOB-GRADIO-25: Several GitHub Actions workflows in the Gradio repository use third-party actions pinned to tags or branch names instead of full commit SHAs. This could allow malicious actors to silently modify actions, potentially leading to tampering with application releases or leaking secrets.

Separately, a GitHub security researcher reported that our GitHub actions could allow untrusted code execution and secret exfiltration if an attacker triggered a workflow and cleverly dumped the memory of GitHub runners.

We’re very grateful to Trail of Bits for the comprehensive security audit of Gradio and for validating the mitigations that we put in place for Gradio 5.

Going forward, we are planning to continue working with the security community to identify and mitigate security issues in Gradio. We have also added security unit tests to our test suite, fuzzer tests specifically designed to identify potential vulnerabilities, and are using static analysis tools like Semgrep in our CI to detect common security issues in our code and prevent security regressions.

We are committed to ensuring that as we continue to develop Gradio 5 (and we have lots of plans!), we do so in a manner that prioritizes security so that we can do our part in making machine learning applications better and safer.

And start building your first Gradio 5 application.

#10869. How to Build a Typed AI Pipeline With Jev and Clairic.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A support email lands: "Order NW-47790, the tent poles snapped on the first night, I paid $389 and I want every cent back today or I'm disputing the charge."

To act on that, your code needs answers to a handful of small questions. Is it a refund request? How urgent is it? Should a person handle it? What's the order number? How much money is involved? It's the same problem whether you're sorting a support inbox or building a custom chatbot that has to work out what each customer is asking for.

The usual move is to send the whole email to a chat model with a prompt that ends "respond in JSON", then validate whatever comes back. It works, but you're paying a model built to write essays to fill in five fields, and you're parsing its guess at a schema.

System One models are built for exactly this kind of job. In this tutorial we'll build a small support inbox pipeline with two of them: Jev from TypeSafe makes the decisions, and Clairic from Cloudflare reads the values. Plain TypeScript then turns their answers into an action. No prompt engineering for output formats, and no JSON repair.

The name comes from Daniel Kahneman's Thinking, Fast and Slow. System 1 is the fast, intuitive kind of thinking you use to read a face or a sign. System 2 is the slow, deliberate kind you use for long division.

A System One model is an AI model that understands natural language but doesn't generate text. You give it some input (the state) and a set of typed questions, and it gives back typed answers with probabilities. There's no free text to parse, because the model can only answer in the shape you asked for.

That's different from asking a chat model for structured output. SitePoint's guide to LLM structured output with JSON Schema shows how to constrain a chat model and validate its JSON with Zod. With a System One model, the type is the interface: a yes/no question comes back as a probability, a pick-one question comes back as one of your options, and a date comes back as a date.

Jev and Clairic are both System One models, but they do different jobs, and that's what makes them a good pair.

Jev can't hand you an order number, and Clairic has no way to pick from a list of options or answer yes or no. Give each one the job it's built for.

If you've read SitePoint's Jev and LangChain tutorial, you've seen Jev deciding which model handles an agent's request. Here we'll use it on the incoming text itself.

Five made-up emails for a made-up outdoor gear store go in. For each one:

Both models read the same email, so they run at the same time.

Put the three values in your environment:

No SDKs are needed. Both models are a single fetch call.

Here's the test inbox. Each email is there to test a different path through the rules:

Jev takes a state (the email) and a set of named questions. We'll ask three, one of each type:

All three questions go in one request. Jev reads the email once and answers every question in parallel, so adding a question costs very little:

We pin jev-1.14.0 rather than the jev-latest alias. Your thresholds get tuned against one version's probabilities, so you want to choose when that version changes.

For the angry tent email, Jev came back with:

(Trimmed: the real response also includes the probability of every option and level.)

Clairic takes the same state, plus a set of typed fields instead of questions:

reference_date anchors relative dates like "the 14th" or "last Monday". In production, pass the date the email arrived.

Each answer comes back with three things worth using:

For the "where is it?" email, Clairic read the deadline like this:

"The 14th" became a full date, worked out from the reference date. Text fields like order_number also come back as character spans of the original email. The value is copied from the input, not generated, so it can't invent an order number that isn't there.

The two models don't depend on each other, so send both requests together:

The time for each email is whichever model is slower, not the two added together.

This is the part a chat model usually ends up doing badly: the business rules. Here they're ordinary code you can read, test, and change without touching a prompt:

Notice that the model's confidence sits right next to the business rule. A $18.95 refund is only automatic if Clairic is sure about both the order number and the amount. Raising the refund limit or the confidence bar is a one-line change, and you don't need to call either model again to see what it would do. Save the answers and replay them.

Every email went where it should. The whole run used 2,703 input tokens on Jev and 2,292 on Clairic, about US$0.0003 in total. At that rate, 10,000 support emails would cost roughly US$0.70.

The interesting part of the run wasn't the right answers. It was the two wrong ones.

"From last Monday." The run used 2 November 2026 as the reference date, which is a Monday. "Last Monday" means 26 October, but Clairic answered 2026-11-02, the reference date itself. Its confidence on that answer was 0.54, compared with 0.99 or higher on almost every other value in the run.

"A couple of weeks ago." Clairic turned this into 2026-10-19, which is a fair reading but still a guess. Its confidence was 0.43.

Neither date changed any action, because the rules only trust values at 0.9 or above. That's the habit to build: a value under your bar counts as unknown. A chat model returning JSON would have handed you "2026-11-02" with the same certainty as everything else.

One more catch: Clairic copied the order number as #NW-48213, hash included, because that's how the customer wrote it. Text values are spans of the input, so normalising them is your code's job. That's one line of code.

System One models handle the reading and the routing. They don't hold a conversation. Once an email is routed, something still has to write the reply, ask a follow-up question, or explain a returns policy in the customer's own words. That's where a chat model earns its cost.

The split that works is: System One models decide, code applies the rules, and a chat model only gets the cases where words matter.

We built a support inbox triage pipeline from two small models and some ordinary code:

Each email took about half a second and cost less than a hundredth of a cent. Most importantly, the two answers that would have been wrong came back flagged as unsure.

The full code is about 160 lines with no dependencies. Try adding a fourth Jev question (does the customer mention a photo?) or an estimate field in Clairic (how many days until the trip?), and see how little the rest of the pipeline has to change.

#10868. Introducing the AMD 5th Gen EPYC™ CPU

AMD has just unveiled its 5th generation of server-grade EPYC CPU based on Zen5 architecture - also known as Turin. It provides a significant boost in performance, especially with a higher number of core count reaching up to 192 and 384 threads.

From Large Language Models (LLMs) to RAG scenarios, Hugging Face users can leverage this new generation of servers to enhance their performance capabilities:

During the last few weeks, we have been working with AMD to validate that the Hugging Face ecosystem is fully supported on this new CPU generation and delivers the expected performance across different tasks.

Also, we have been cooking some exciting new ways to leverage torch.compile for AMD CPU through the use of AMD ZenDNN PyTorch plugin (zentorch) to speed up even more the kind of workloads we will be discussing after.

While we were able to get early access to this work to test Hugging Face models and libraries and share with you performance, we expect AMD to make it soon available to the community - stay tuned!

In this section, we present the results from our benchmarking of the two AMD EPYC CPUs: Turin (128 cores) and Genoa (96 cores). For these benchmarks, we utilized the ZenDNN plug-in for PyTorch (zentorch), which provides inference optimizations tailored for deep learning workloads on AMD EPYC CPUs. This plug-in integrates seamlessly with the torch.compile graph compilation flow, enabling multiple passes of graph-level optimizations on the torch.fx graph to achieve further performance acceleration.

To ensure optimal performance, we used the bfloat16 data type and employed ZenDNN 5.0. We configured multi-instance setups that enable the parallel execution of multiple Meta LLaMA 3.1 8B model instances spawning across all the cores. Each model instance is allocated 32 physical cores per socket, allowing us to leverage the full processing power of the servers for efficient data handling and computational speed.

We ran the benchmarks using two different batch sizes—16 and 32—across five distinct use cases:

These configurations not only facilitate a comprehensive analysis of how each server performs under varying workloads but also simulate real-world applications of LLMs. Specifically, we plot the decode throughput (excluding the first token) for each use case, to illustrate performance differences.

Throughput results for Meta Llama 3.1 8B, comparing AMD Turin against AMD Genoa. AMD Turin consistently outperforms the AMD Genoa CPUs, achieving approximately 2X higher throughput in most configurations.

As demonstrated, the AMD EPYC Turin CPU offers a significant boost in performance for AI use cases compared to its predecessor, the AMD Genoa. To enhance reproducibility and streamline the benchmarking process, we utilized optimum-benchmark, which provides a unified framework for efficient benchmarking across various setups. This enabled us to effectively benchmark using the zentorch backend for torch.compile.

Furthermore, we have developed an optimized Dockerfile that will be released soon, along with the benchmarking code. This will facilitate easy deployment and reproduction of our results, ensuring that others can effectively leverage our findings.

You can find more information at AMD Zen Deep Neural Network (ZenDNN)

#10867. Fixing Gradient Accumulation

Our friends at Unsloth shared an issue regarding gradient accumulation yesterday that is affecting the transformers Trainer. The initial report comes from @bnjmn_marie (kudos to him!).

Gradient accumulation is supposed to be mathematically equivalent to full batch training; however, losses did not match between training runs where the setting was toggled on and off.

Inside the modeling code of each model, transformers offers a "default" loss function that's the most typically used one for the model's task. It is determined by what the modeling class should be used for: question answering, token classification, causal LM, masked LM.

This is the default loss function and it was not meant to be customizable: it is only computed when labels and input_ids are passed as inputs to the model, so the user doesn't have to compute the loss. The default loss is useful but is limited by design: for anything different being done, we expect the labels to not be passed directly, and for users to get the logits back from the model and use them to compute the loss outside of the model.

However, the transformers Trainer, as well as many Trainers, heavily leverage these methods because of the simplicity it offers: it is a double-edged sword. Providing a simple API that becomes different as the use-case differs is not a well-thought out API, and we've been caught by surprise ourselves.

To be precise, for gradient accumulation across token-level tasks like causal LM training, the correct loss should be computed by the total loss across all batches in a gradient accumulation step divided by the total number of all non padding tokens in those batches. This is not the same as the average of the per-batch loss values. The fix is quite simple, see the following:

To address this issue, we’re changing the way our models and training work in two ways:

All model that inherit from PreTrainedModel now have a loss_function property, which is determined by either:

We are working to ship the first change for the most popular models in this PR: https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/34191#pullrequestreview-2372725010. Following this, a call for contributions to help propagate this to the rest of the models will be done so that the majority of models is supported by next release.

We are also actively working to ship the second change in this PR: https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/34198, which will allow users to use their own loss function and make use of the number of samples seen per-batch to help with calculating their loss (and will perform the correct loss calculation during gradient accumulation as more models are supported from the prior change)

By tomorrow, you should expect the Trainer to behave correctly with gradient accumulation. Please install from main in order to benefit from the fix then:

In general, we are very responsive to bug reports submitted to our issue tracker: https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/issues

This issue has been in Transformers for some time as it's mostly a default that should be updated by the end-user; however, when defaults become non-intuitive, they are bound to be changed. In this instance, we've updated the code and shipped a fix in less than 24 hours, which is what we aim for issues like this one in transformers. Please, come and submit your issues if you have some; this is the only way we can get transformers to improve and fit well within your different use-cases.

The key takeaway is that gradient accumulation can make training with large effective batch sizes much more practical when GPU memory is limited. The numerical details around loss scaling are especially useful for avoiding subtle training bugs.

#10865. Porting the NDK “Endless Tunnel” to iOS: A Masterclass in Cross-Platform C++

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

When developers talk about high-performance mobile games, the Android NDK samples by Bruno Oliveira are often cited as the gold standard for clean, low-level C++. But as an iOS developer, I wanted to see if I could take that same “pure” C++ logic and make it sing on an iPhone.

My latest project, TunnelFeveriOS, is the result of that journey. It isn’t just a port; it’s a blueprint for building a custom game engine.

The original Endless Tunnel is built to live within the Android lifecycle (JNI, Activity, and NDK). Moving this to iOS required more than just hitting “compile.” I had to build a Platform Abstraction Layer.

To make the C++ engine talk to the iOS UI, I utilized Objective-C++ (.mm** files)**. This allowed me to keep the game's high-speed math and geometry in native C++ while using Cocoa Touch to manage the windowing and touch input. In TunnelFeveriOS, you’ll see how the view controller manages the game loop, feeding time deltas and touch coordinates directly into the C++ core.

Since the original game uses OpenGL ES, I leveraged iOS’s GLKit framework. The trick was ensuring that the shaders and vertex buffer objects (VBOs) originally written for Android were correctly initialized within the iOS EAGLContext. The result? 60 FPS performance that feels native because, at the machine level, it is.

A port is only “production-ready” if it handles modern app requirements. I integrated Google Mobile Ads (AdMob) to trigger Interstitial ads during game-over states.

This presented a unique threading challenge:

I implemented a messaging system that allows the C++ core to “request” an ad, which the Objective-C wrapper then catches and executes on the main thread — preventing the game from hanging or crashing.

This project proves that you don’t need a heavy engine like Unity or Unreal to achieve cross-platform results. By keeping the “brain” of your game in C++ and building thin “shells” for each platform (Android NDK or iOS/XCode), you gain:

If you’re interested in how to bridge the gap between low-level C++ and high-level iOS development, check out the full source code here:

Now that the foundation is laid, I’m looking into implementing a Metal-based renderer to fully embrace the future of Apple graphics. If you’ve worked on C++ to Metal bridges, I’d love to hear your thoughts in the comments!

#10864. Deploying Speech-to-Speech on Hugging Face

Speech-to-Speech (S2S) is an exciting new project from Hugging Face that combines several advanced models to create a seamless, almost magical experience: you speak, and the system responds with a synthesized voice.

The project implements a cascaded pipeline leveraging models available through the Transformers library on the Hugging Face hub. The pipeline consists of the following components:

What's more, S2S has multi-language support! It currently supports English, French, Spanish, Chinese, Japanese, and Korean. You can run the pipeline in single-language mode or use the auto flag for automatic language detection. Check out the repo for more details here.

Running Speech-to-Speech requires significant computational resources. Even on a high-end laptop you might encounter latency issues, particularly when using the most advanced models. While a powerful GPU can mitigate these problems, not everyone has the means (or desire!) to set up their own hardware.

This is where Hugging Face's Inference Endpoints (IE) come into play. Inference Endpoints allow you to rent a virtual machine equipped with a GPU (or other hardware you might need) and pay only for the time your system is running, providing an ideal solution for deploying performance-heavy applications like Speech-to-Speech.

In this blog post, we’ll guide you step by step to deploy Speech-to-Speech to a Hugging Face Inference Endpoint. This is what we'll cover:

Inference Endpoints provide a scalable and efficient way to deploy machine learning models. These endpoints allow you to serve models with minimal setup, leveraging a variety of powerful hardware. Inference Endpoints are ideal for deploying applications that require high performance and reliability, without the need to manage underlying infrastructure.

Here's a few key features, and be sure to check out the documentation for more:

Inference Endpoints supports all of the Transformers and Sentence-Transformers tasks, but can also support custom tasks. These are the IE setup options:

For simpler models, options 1 and 2 are ideal and make deploying with Inference Endpoints super straightforward. However, for a complex pipeline like S2S, you will need the flexibility of option 3: deploying our IE using a custom Docker image.

This method not only provides more flexibility but also improved performance by optimizing the build process and gathering necessary data. If you’re dealing with complex model pipelines or want to optimize your application deployment, this guide will offer valuable insights.

To begin creating a custom Docker image, we started by cloning Hugging Face’s default Docker image repository. This serves as a great starting point for deploying machine learning models in inference tasks.

You can check out all of our changes here

With the repository cloned, the next step was tailoring the image to support our Speech-to-Speech pipeline.

To integrate the project smoothly, we added the speech-to-speech codebase and any required datasets as submodules. This approach offers better version control, ensuring the exact version of the code and data is always available when the Docker image is built.

By including data directly within the Docker container, we avoid having to download it each time the endpoint is instantiated, which significantly reduces startup time and ensures the system is reproducible. The data is stored in a Hugging Face repository, which provides easy tracking and versioning.

Next, we modified the Dockerfile to suit our needs:

Once the modifications were in place, we built and pushed the custom image to Docker Hub:

With the Docker image built and pushed, it’s ready to be used in the Hugging Face Inference Endpoint. By using this pre-built image, the endpoint can launch faster and run more efficiently, as all dependencies and data are pre-packaged within the image.

Using a custom docker image just requires a slightly different configuration, feel free to check out the documentation. We will walk through the approach to do this in both the GUI and the API.

The Model Repository doesn't actually matter since the models are specified and downloaded in the container creation, but Inference Endpoints requires a model, so feel free to pick a slim one of your choice.

You need to specify HF_TOKEN because we need to download gated models in the container creation stage. This won't be necessary if you use models that aren't gated or private.

The current huggingface-inference-toolkit entrypoint uses port 5000 as default, but the inference endpoint expects port 80. You should match this in the Container Port. We already set it in our dockerfile, but beware if making your own from scratch!

Here we will walk through the steps for creating the endpoint with the API. Just use this code in your python environment of choice.

Use a token that can write an endpoint (Write or Fine-Grained)

To use the endpoint, we will need to build a small webservice. The code for it is done on s2s_handler.py in the speech_to_speech library which we use for the client and webservice_starlette.py in thespeech_to_speech_inference_toolkit which we used to build the docker image. Normally, you would only have a custom handler for an endpoint, but since we want to have a really low latency, we also built the webservice to support websocket connections instead of normal requests. This sounds intimidating at first, but the webservice is only 32 lines of code!

This code will run prepare_handler on startup, which will initialize all the models and warm them up. Then, each message will be processed by inference_handler.process_streaming_data

This method simply receives the audio data from the client, chunks it into small parts for the VAD, and submits it to a queue for processing. Then it checks the output processing queue (the spoken response from the model!) and returns it if there is something. All of the internal processing is handled by Hugging Face's speech_to_speech library.

The webservice receives and returns audio. But there is still a big missing piece, how do we record and play back the audio? For that, we created a client that connects to the service. The easiest is to divide the analysis in the connection to the webservice and the recording/playing of audio.

Initializing the webservice client requires setting a header for all messages with our Hugging Face Token. When initializing the client, we set what we want to do on common messages (open, close, error, message). This will determine what our client does when the server sends it messages.

We can see that the reactions to the messages are straight forward, with the on_message being the only method with more complexity. This method understands when the server is done responding and starts 'listening' back to the user. Otherwise, it puts the data from the server in the playback queue.

The audio is recorded on the audio_input_callback method, it simply submits all chunks to a queue. Then, it is sent to the server with the send_audio method. Here, if there is no audio to send, we still submit an empty array in order to receive a response from the server. The responses from the server are handled by the on_message method we saw earlier in the blog. Then, the playback of the audio responses are handled by the audio_output_callback method. Here we only need to ensure that the audio is in the range we expect (We don't want to destroy someone eardrum's because of a faulty package!) and ensure that the size of the output array is what the playback library expects.

In this post, we walked through the steps of deploying the Speech-to-Speech (S2S) pipeline on Hugging Face Inference Endpoints using a custom Docker image. We built a custom container to handle the complexities of the S2S pipeline and demonstrated how to configure it for scalable, efficient deployment. Hugging Face Inference Endpoints make it easier to bring performance-heavy applications like Speech-to-Speech to life, without the hassle of managing hardware or infrastructure.

#10863. Releasing Outlines-core 0.1.0: structured generation in Rust and Python

dottxt and Hugging Face are excited to announce that we have been collaborating on outlines-core, a Rust port of outlines’s core algorithms for structured generation. On top of getting reliable output from LLMs with outlines, this Rust port offers several further benefits to users of outlines:

These improvements should not only improve the performance for existing outlines users, but also dramatically increase the ways users can incorporate structured generation into their LLM workflows. outlines-core is now public, integrated in outlines, and the version 0.1.0 of the Python bindings are out. You can find the repo here.

Structured generation means that your LLM is guaranteed to follow a desired format. This could be JSON, a Pydantic Model, a regular expression or a context-free grammar. The key is that structured generation forbids the 'wrong' tokens from being generated.

Let’s take an extremely simple example. The LLM should generate a boolean, “true” or “false”. And nothing more. For the sake of illustration, let’s say that LLMs generate characters instead of tokens. So the first character is ", we can just skip the forward pass. For the second, we don’t need to sample from all possible characters. The LLM should just choose between t or f.

After that, regardless of the path we take, there is only one valid next character. If the LLM chose t as the first character, then it has to follow with r, u and e. And similarly if it chose f it follows with a, l, s, e. And will choose the last " as the final character regardless of the path. There is of course more under the hood, for more in-depth coverage we recommend this dottxt blog and the associated paper on arxiv.

It might not immediately be obvious how amazing structured generation can be. The first use-case many think of is “nice, now my LLM can return valid JSON, so I can treat it as an API and serialize/deserialize JSON reliably”. But that’s just scratching the surface. When you think about it, structure is everywhere, even in places where you least expect it like the GSM8K benchmark.

These are just a few examples of what structured generation enables:

And, perhaps more surprising, it reduces the sensitivity of evaluations to the specific prompt being used and the number of shots. Apart from the amazing tricks that structure gives you, it’s also more performant. The dottxt blog has many good articles with performance benchmarks.

Probably the first thing that comes to your mind when you hear “rewrite in Rust” is performance. And yes, that’s the case for outlines-core as well. Several key parts are yet to be moved over to Rust, and despite that, we already see an average 2x improvement in compilation speed.

Before the Rust port, Outlines used Numba to accelerate the building of the index. While Numba is fast (the runtime performance is comparable to Rust), the JIT-compilation of the Numba functions added a source of latency during the first run, which was a source of frustration for many users. Using Rust means we can compile the index building functions ahead of time, adding no latency during the first run. While this was not important in a production context (since the first run could anyways be done as part of deployment), it can make a huge difference during the experimentation phase!

One of the main reasons for rewriting Outlines in Rust is the emphasis on safety and reliability that Rust brings to the table. Rust's strong static typing, combined with Rust's ownership model, eliminate entire classes of bugs, such as null pointer dereferences and data races in concurrent code. This leads to more robust and secure software.

In the context of Outlines, safety is crucial. Structured generation often involves complex data structures and manipulations, especially when dealing with high-performance inference engines. By leveraging Rust's safety guarantees, we reduce the risk of runtime errors and undefined behaviors that can arise from memory mismanagement.

Additionally, Rust's compile-time checks encourage developers to write cleaner and more maintainable code. This improves the current codebase and makes future development more efficient. New contributors can onboard more quickly, and the code is easier to audit and verify for correctness.

Outlines was designed to do more than providing the core algorithms for structured generation. Among other things, it includes integrations to other libraries like transformers which mean the library packs many dependencies. Separating the core algorithms from the Outlines library means that other libraries wishing to include structured generation can do so by importing a very lightweight library. So we can imagine in the near future libraries such as transformers and llama-cpp-python integrating structured generation directly. This allows the dottxt team to focus on the core algorithms.

Most of LLM training is written in Python, but inference is slightly different. It happens on many different devices, on specialized servers and is written in a range of programming languages. This is why portability also matters for structured generation. By having the core functionality of outlines written in rust, we can now create bindings to other languages.

For example, this port makes the integration into the text-generation-inference much smoother. TGI’s server logic is written in Rust, and we want to avoid having to call Python code as much as we possibly can. It also means libraries like mistral.rs or models implemented using candle can benefit from Outlines’s performance and capabilities.

In the future we plan to explore bindings to JS/TS, allowing outlines to be used in transformers-js. Or potentially Swift bindings, making outlines natively usable on Apple devices. But for now the focus is going to be on the Python bindings, and continuing to make outlines-core’s feature set complete by expanding support for the JSON Schema specification.

Do you like working with structured generation, parsers, making LLMs output only valid JSON? Star the library, tweet about it, join in and contribute! Share your work on Twitter, and with dottxt’s and Hugging Face's community.

#10862. How Product Teams Can Use AI User Research to Test Assumptions Before Sprint Planning

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Sprint planning is on Thursday, and the top of the backlog rests on three things nobody has checked. Users want the feature, they will find it, and they will understand what it does when they do. Each belief is plausible, and each has already been written into a ticket.

AI user research uses language models to simulate or analyze user conversations, so a team can put a question to a modeled audience in minutes instead of recruiting people for weeks. Used well, it gives a product team a cheap first check on backlog assumptions. Used badly, it produces confident-sounding agreement. This guide covers a two-day routine that gets the benefit and avoids the trap.

An assumption is worth testing when the plan depends on it and a wrong answer would change the ticket. "Users like clean interfaces" fails that test. "Analysts re-apply the same filters every session" passes, because if it is false the saved-filters feature shrinks or disappears.

The timing matters because planning leaves little room for research. The Scrum Guide says Sprint Planning is timeboxed to a maximum of eight hours for a one-month Sprint, and the first question the team answers is why the Sprint is valuable. Checks run before that meeting inform the answer. Checks run during it eat the time meant for deciding.

Write each risky item as a short card that names the belief, the consequence of being wrong, and the decision it feeds. A card forces the team to say what would change its mind, which most tickets never do. Here is an example:

Aim for three to five cards. A team that tries to test the whole backlog will test none of it, and the cards on the riskiest items give the best return.

AI user research comes in two forms. The first analyzes data you already hold: clustering support tickets and summarizing interview transcripts. It works on real evidence, so its main risk is a sloppy summary.

The second form interviews simulated people. AI user research of this kind builds a panel of modeled personas matched to your target profile, asks them your questions, and reports the themes. It needs no recruiting and returns results quickly, which fits a two-day window. Its output comes from a model of users and not from users, and that distinction should appear in every planning document that cites it.

A simulated audience helps most when you want to sharpen a question, and least when you need proof. Nielsen Norman Group's 2024 review of synthetic users found them useful for generating hypotheses and preparing interview guides. It warned against using them for final decisions or concept validation, and for niche populations, because AI tends to please and "every idea is often seen as a good one."

Spend Tuesday collecting answers and Wednesday reading them skeptically. On Tuesday, put each card's question to the modeled audience in neutral wording, and ask what would make them not use the feature. A question phrased as "Would saved filters help you?" invites a yes, while "Walk me through setting up your weekly report" does not.

On Wednesday, compare the answers with what you already know from support tickets and analytics. Mark each assumption as supported, contradicted, or unclear. Treat a unanimous answer with suspicion, because real audiences rarely agree on anything. Also be wary of lists in which the modeled users "seem to care about everything," which is how Nielsen Norman Group describes their weak prioritization.

Whatever stays unclear or high risk goes to real people. Jakob Nielsen's classic analysis found that five users find about 85% of usability problems, assuming comparable users, and he recommended several small rounds over one large one. An AI check is a good way to decide what those five people should be asked.

Each mark maps to a different decision. A contradicted assumption means the ticket is cut or reduced to its smallest useful version. A supported assumption that rests only on simulated evidence is not yet safe, so schedule a real-user check as the first task in the sprint, ahead of the build work that depends on it. An unclear assumption should not receive full scope.

The cost of skipping this step is real. A 2019 analysis of 615 product subscriptions by a product analytics vendor found that about 12% of features generate 80% of daily usage volume, and 80% of features are rarely or never used. That is one vendor's customer base, and the figures cover features that customers chose to track, so treat them as a rough guide. They still suggest that most of a backlog is a bet.

AI user research cannot replace talking to real users. Nielsen Norman Group found that synthetic users gave overly optimistic accounts of their own behavior, such as claiming to finish every course in a study, and that they cannot supply real past experience. It also called presenting synthetic findings as real-user findings "an unethical way to share what you've learned."

Two habits keep a team honest. Label every piece of evidence in the planning document as modeled, observed, or reported, and require that any feature built on modeled evidence has a real-user check scheduled. The review also warned that teams starting with synthetic research may get comfortable and skip the real kind, so put the real check on the calendar before the first AI result arrives.

Can AI user research replace interviews with real users? No. It is a cheap first pass that helps you write better questions and spot weak assumptions. Anything that drives a significant build still needs real people.

How many assumptions should a team test before planning? Three to five. Pick the ones where a wrong answer would cut or reshape a ticket.

How do I stop simulated users from just agreeing with me? Use neutral, open questions, ask what would make them avoid the feature, and treat unanimous answers as a warning sign.

What should I do with results I cannot verify? Mark them as modeled, give them less weight than observed evidence, and schedule a real-user check before committing full scope.

Sources: Scrum Guide, Sprint Planning; Jakob Nielsen, "Why You Only Need to Test with 5 Users" (March 18, 2000); Nielsen Norman Group, "Synthetic Users: If, When, and How to Use AI-Generated 'Research'" (June 21, 2024); 2019 Feature Adoption Report (615 product subscriptions, vendor-reported).

WebGPU is a new web standard for accelerated graphics and compute. WebGPU is the successor to WebGL and provides significantly better performance, because it allows for more direct interaction with modern GPUs. #10859. AI-Powered Pentesting for DevSecOps: 7 Checks Developers Should Make First

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Security testing used to happen once or twice a year, usually after a release had already shipped. That rhythm does not fit teams that deploy daily. AI-assisted tools now promise testing that runs continuously, chains steps together on its own, and writes up what it found.

For developers, the interesting question is not whether these tools are impressive. It is what has to be true in your pipeline before you let an automated attacker loose on your own systems. This article covers seven checks to make first, each with a pass condition, and one short code example you can run. Some checks, such as written authorization and cost tracking, usually belong to a security lead or manager. For those, the developer's job is to confirm they exist, not to own them.

Testing systems you do not have permission to test is not a gray area. Make sure someone with authority has approved the targets and the time window, and keep that approval with your records. Run the first tests against staging with test data. Production comes later, once you know how the tool behaves and what load it creates.

Pass: The approval is on file, and the SOC knows the window and source IPs.

An automated tester should never decide for itself what it is allowed to touch. Define scope in a file that your pipeline can check: which hosts are in bounds, when testing may run, and whether anything destructive is allowed.

SitePoint's article on security patterns for autonomous agents uses an open-source AI penetration-testing agent as its case study. It covers sandboxed execution, tool permissions scoped to each role, approval gates for high-risk actions, and audit logging. Scope enforcement belongs in that same family of controls. Here is a minimal check that refuses any target outside the allowlist or time window:

Call this before every scan job, and log the result. A tool that is out of bounds should fail loudly instead of quietly continuing.

Pass: An out-of-scope target fails the job, and egress outside the allowlist is blocked.

Findings are only useful if they reach the people who can fix them. Most teams already have a place where security results show up in pull requests or a security tab. SitePoint's walkthrough on automating DevSecOps static analysis with GitHub Actions shows how results written in the SARIF format appear as inline annotations and can block a merge when severity crosses a threshold. If your pentest tool can export SARIF or a similar format, send its findings to the same place.

Pass: The tool exports SARIF or similar, and results show up in PRs or the security tab.

An AI tool can produce a long list of findings. To judge whether they are complete and sensible, you need a reference for what good web security testing covers. The OWASP Web Security Testing Guide is a free, widely used checklist of test categories for web applications. It covers web applications only, so APIs and network services exposed to the internet need their own coverage. Map the tool's findings against it, and note which categories it never touched.

Pass: You know which OWASP WSTG categories you expect the tool to cover.

Vendors describe AI pentesting in similar terms: agents plan attack steps, try them, and verify what works. For a view of how a security vendor explains the approach, CyCognito's overview of AI penetration testing walks through a workflow from scoping to autonomous testing, validation and reporting, and notes that human review stays part of the process. All vendor claims need testing in a demo against your own systems before you rely on them.

Ask the same questions of any tool you evaluate: What does it test beyond known checks? How does it confirm a finding is real? What does it send to external services?

Pass: The vendor has clear answers, including where the target list comes from.

Automated findings need review. A person should confirm that a reported path is exploitable, judge its business impact, and decide the fix order. Make sure this is set up before the first run. Without it, a team can end up with a long backlog of unverified findings and little trust in the tool.

Pass: There is a named reviewer and time set aside each cycle.

Running agents continuously can add up, especially when they call large models. Make sure you can track what each run costs and how many real issues it finds, so you can compare it with other approaches. You also need to be able to rerun the specific test that found a problem after a fix ships and keep the result. A finding is only closed when the retest passes.

Pass: Both are possible before you commit to running the tool continuously.

Does AI pentesting replace manual penetration testing?

Not entirely. Automated testing can run more often and cover more ground, but people are still needed for scoping, complex attack paths and judging impact.

In staging, with test data, inside a written scope and time window.

What should I do with findings from the tool?

Send them to the same place as your other security results, have the named reviewer check them, and retest after fixes.

AI-assisted pentesting can give development teams faster and more frequent security feedback, but only when it runs inside clear limits. Before the first run, check that targets and the window are approved, scope is enforced by your pipeline, findings will land where developers work, you have a baseline to judge the output, you know what the tool tests and sends out, someone owns the review, and you can measure cost and retest. The scope check above is small, but it makes sure the tool stays inside the lines you set.

We are pleased to announce our partnership with Protect AI, as part of our long-standing commitment to provide a safe and reliable platform for the ML community.

Protect AI is a company founded with a mission to create a safer AI-powered world. They are developing powerful tools, namely Guardian, to ensure that the rapid pace of AI innovation can continue without compromising security.

Our decision to partner with Protect AI stems from their community driven approach to security, active support of open source, and expertise in all things security x AI.

Interested in joining our security partnership / providing scanning information on the Hub? Please get in touch with us over at security@huggingface.co.

To share models, we serialize weights, configs and other data structures we use to interact with the models, in order to facilitate storage and transport. Some serialization formats are vulnerable to nasty exploits, such as arbitrary code execution (looking at you pickle), making shared models that use those formats potentially dangerous.

As Hugging Face has become a popular platform for model sharing, we’d like to help protect the community from this, hence why we have developed tools like picklescan and why we are integrating Guardian in our scanner suite.

Pickle is not the only exploitable format out there, see for reference how one can exploit Keras Lambda layers to achieve arbitrary code execution. The good news is that Guardian catches both of these exploits and more in additional file formats – see their Knowledge Base for up to date scanner information.

Read all our documentation on security here: https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/security 🔥

All public model repositories will be scanned by Guardian automatically as soon as you push your files to the Hub. Here is an example repository you can check out to see the feature in action: mcpotato/42-eicar-street.

Note that you might not see a scan for your model as of today, as we have over 1 million model repos. It may take us some time to catch up 😅.

In total, we have already scanned hundreds of millions of files, because we believe that empowering the community to share models in a safe and frictionless manner will lead to growth for the whole field.

Part of the secret sauce behind it is that it relies on movie clips from YouTube and Q&A distilled from precise audio descriptions designed for visually impaired audiences. These descriptions offer rich context beyond basic visuals (e.g., "What color is the car?"), helping us create more complex questions.

To automate question creation, we first built question templates by inspecting existing datasets like MovieQA and TVQA. We clustered the questions in these datasets using a textual similarity model WhereIsAI/UAE-Large-V1 and then prompted GPT-4 with 10 random examples from each cluster to generate a question template and a prototypical question for each:

Since templates aren't always relevant to every movie clip, we used Gemini 1.0 Pro to select the most appropriate ones for each scene. Next, we feed a language model the scene's text, selected template names (e.g., "Physical Possession"), sample questions, and a system prompt to create scene-specific questions. A well-designed prompt helps the model focus on the entire scene, generating deeper questions while avoiding superficial ones. We found that:

Using this approach, we generate approximately 32 questions per video. Prior to releasing CinePile, we implemented several mechanisms to ensure the quality of the dataset/benchmark that we cover in the next section.

Through continued use of the benchmark by our team and the broader community, we identified several areas for improvement that drove us to consider CinePile 2.0.

For CinePile's second release, we worked together with Hugging Face (following their successful experimentation with fine-tuning Video Llava 7B on CinePile) to identify and prioritize several areas of improvement.

To address these issues, we introduced a new Adversarial Refinement pipeline that helps improve weak questions rather than simply discarding them. This approach can be more easily applied at scale. Throughout this post, we'll refer to the model(s) that identify degenerate questions (using only the question and answer choices, without visual or dialogue information) as the "Deaf-Blind LLM."

The Adversarial Refinement pipeline aims to modify questions or answers until a Deaf-Blind LLM cannot easily predict the correct answer. Here's how it works:
