#10836. Why Your AI Agent Can't Read the Web (and How to Build a Fetch Layer That Can)

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

This is the least glamorous part of building with LLMs and it's where a lot of agent projects quietly fall over. The model is rarely the problem. The fetch is. In this article we'll look at why live web retrieval has become so unreliable for AI tools, what the numbers say about the shift, and how to build a small, well-behaved fetch layer in Python that fails loudly instead of feeding your model garbage.

A few years ago, a plain requests.get() worked on most of the public web. That's no longer true, and the reason is simple: there are now more bots than people.

According to the 2025 Imperva Bad Bot Report, automated traffic made up 51% of all web traffic in 2024. That's the first time in a decade it has passed human activity. Bad bots alone (scrapers, credential stuffers, scalpers) went from 32% to 37% of traffic in a single year.

Source: Imperva Bad Bot Report 2024 and 2025

From a site owner's point of view, your polite research agent and a credential-stuffing botnet look much the same at the network edge. Both are non-browser clients making fast requests from data-center IP ranges. So the defaults have tightened. In July 2025 Cloudflare began blocking known AI crawlers by default for new customers, and bot management products now look at TLS fingerprints, header order, IP reputation and JavaScript execution, not just the User-Agent string.

It helps to understand the publisher's side of the deal, because it explains why your agent is being treated with suspicion.

Cloudflare splits AI crawling into three purposes: training (collecting data to train models), search (building an index for AI search answers) and user action (fetching a page because a person just asked a question). Training dominates.

Training crawls take content and send nothing back. Cloudflare measures this with a crawl-to-referral ratio: how many pages a platform crawls for every visitor it sends to the site. In its crawl-to-click gap analysis, the ratios for some AI platforms ran into the tens of thousands, compared with single digits for traditional search.

If you ran a publication and saw those numbers, you'd block too. The catch is that blocking is usually done by user agent or IP range, so it hits user-action fetches as well. Those are the ones that happen when a person asks your agent to read a specific article, and Cloudflare's 2025 Year in Review found they grew more than 15x during the year. Your agent is caught in a fight it didn't start.

The mix of crawlers also shifts quickly, which makes static allow and block lists fragile on both sides:

And restrictions keep piling up. The Consent in Crisis study audited 14,000 web domains and found that a large and fast-growing share of the sources behind the C4 training corpus now restrict AI crawlers, either through robots.txt or their terms of service.

Source: Longpre et al., Consent in Crisis (NeurIPS 2024)

So that's the environment your agent fetches in. Here's how to build for it.

Before writing any retry logic, put names on your failures. "The request failed" is useless to both you and the model. In practice almost every failed fetch falls into one of four buckets:

Bucket 2 is the dangerous one, because a block page often comes back with a 200 OK. If you don't check, the model will happily summarise "Checking your browser before accessing..." as if it were the article.

Here's a compact fetch layer in Python using httpx and the standard library's robots.txt parser. It's around 100 lines and covers the four buckets above.

Use a descriptive user agent with a contact URL. It costs you nothing and site operators are far more likely to allow a client they can identify and reach. Then check robots.txt (standardised as RFC 9309) before every new host.

The lru_cache means you fetch robots.txt once per origin rather than once per page. In a long-running service you'll want a cache with a TTL instead, since robots.txt files do change.

This is the core of the layer. Instead of returning raw HTML, return a result that says which bucket you landed in.

The marker list is deliberately simple. It won't catch every interstitial, but it catches the common ones, and a false "blocked" is much cheaper than a confident summary of a CAPTCHA page. Log every blocked result with its first few hundred characters so you can grow the list from real data.

Retries should depend on the bucket. Throttled and broken responses get exponential backoff with jitter. Blocked and not-allowed responses get no retries at all.

Note the cap on wait. A site sending Retry-After: 3600 is telling you to go away for an hour. An interactive agent should report that to the user rather than block a request thread for that long.

The cheapest fetch is the one you don't make. Agents often re-read the same documentation page several times in one session. Store the ETag and Last-Modified headers and send them back as If-None-Match and If-Modified-Since. A 304 Not Modified response costs the server almost nothing and lowers the odds of being rate limited.

Wire these into fetch() by passing headers=conditional_headers(url) to client.get(). On a 304, return the cached text. On a 200, call remember().

Finally, don't hide failures from the LLM. Give the tool output a structured shape so the model can reason about it:

(extract_main_text is whatever readability or boilerplate-removal step you already use. Libraries like trafilatura work well here.)

With this in place, the model's answer changes from a made-up summary to "I couldn't read that page because the site blocks automated access. Here's what I found from two other sources." That's a better product, and it builds trust with users.

Once you've done everything above, some legitimate user-action fetches will still fail. That's usually because the site blocks data-center IP ranges outright, not because of anything your agent did. Teams handle this in a few ways, roughly in order of preference:

The principle is the same in every case: the network path is a reliability decision, not a way around a site's wishes. Your robots.txt check and your honest user agent should stay in place whichever route the request takes.

Once your fetch layer returns structured results, observability is easy. Emit one event per fetch with the host, status bucket and latency, and watch these:

If you're prototyping agents with AI coding assistants, ask them to generate these metrics hooks from the start. They're easy to bolt on now and painful to add later. For a sense of how well current tools handle this kind of infrastructure code, Vibe Coder Journal publishes hands-on reviews and benchmarks of AI coding tools.

The web your agent reads in 2026 isn't the open, fetch-anything web many of us learned on. More than half the traffic is automated, publishers have good reasons to be wary of AI crawlers, and the defaults now lean toward blocking. You can't change that. You can make your agent a good citizen, though: one that identifies itself, respects the rules, backs off when asked, and tells the truth when it can't read something.

Most of the reliability gains come from the unglamorous parts: classifying failures, caching and passing honest errors to the model. Get those right and your agent will feel much more dependable, even on the days when half the web won't let it in.

It depends on the jurisdiction, the site's terms of service and what you do with the content. Respecting robots.txt and site terms is the baseline. For commercial products, get proper legal advice.

Many site owners expect it to, and RFC 9309 makes no exception for user-triggered fetches. The safest default is to obey it and tell the user when a page is disallowed.

Many bot-protection systems serve a challenge page with a 200 status. Check the body for challenge markers before passing it to the model, as in the looks_blocked() function above.

Only for pages that render their main content with JavaScript. Try a plain HTTP fetch first. Headless browsers are slower, cost more to run and are easier to fingerprint.

#10835. How to Use CSS Attribute Selectors to Build More Flexible User Interfaces

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

When developing a website, developers often rely on CSS classes to style buttons, forms, navigation elements, and other interface components. This approach works well, but some situations require styles to depend on an element's HTML attributes rather than additional class names.

CSS attribute selectors provide a practical solution. They allow developers to target elements based on whether an attribute exists, what value it contains, or whether its value matches a particular pattern. Used carefully, they can simplify styling and make reusable components easier to maintain.

An attribute selector targets an HTML element using square brackets. For example, a developer can select every input field that has a required attribute:

This rule applies to inputs with the required attribute, regardless of their input type.

Developers can also target a specific attribute value:

This is useful when different input types need different visual treatments without introducing additional classes into the HTML.

Forms are a practical place to apply attribute selectors because HTML already provides attributes that describe how individual fields behave.

Consider a registration form containing email, password, and telephone fields. Each input can be styled according to its purpose:

The CSS can target these fields independently:

This approach keeps the markup descriptive while allowing the stylesheet to respond to the attributes already present in the document.

One important distinction is that required indicates a validation requirement, while :invalid represents an input's current validity state. These should not be treated as interchangeable.

CSS provides several matching operators that help developers target more specific attribute values.

These operators can be useful when working with links, downloadable files, language attributes, and reusable components.

For example, a website might want to distinguish PDF downloads from ordinary navigation links:

This adds a small visual indicator to links whose URLs end in .pdf.

Attribute selectors can also help identify links with different destinations or behaviors.

For example, external links that use HTTPS can receive a subtle visual indicator:

However, matching an HTTPS URL does not necessarily prove that a link points to an external website. Internal links can also use HTTPS, so developers should consider the actual navigation requirements before applying special styling.

For more examples of selector combinations and matching rules, SitePoint's guide to CSS Attribute Selectors provides a useful reference.

Although attribute selectors are flexible, they should not replace every class-based styling decision.

A selector such as [class*="button"] can match unintended elements if their class names happen to contain the same text. Similarly, broad attribute rules may affect components that were not originally intended to receive those styles.

For predictable results, use exact attribute matching whenever possible and prefer descriptive classes for major component styling.

Developers should also remember that CSS selectors only control presentation. They do not replace JavaScript validation, server-side security checks, or proper HTML semantics.

The MDN documentation on attribute selectors provides further details about selector syntax, matching behavior, and supported operators.

Before adding attribute selectors to a large stylesheet, inspect the affected elements using browser developer tools.

Check whether the selector matches the intended elements.

Test fields with different attribute values.

Verify disabled, required, and invalid form states.

Check navigation links and downloadable files.

Test the layout on mobile and desktop screens.

Review whether existing component styles are being unintentionally overridden.

This process helps identify unexpected matches before they affect the production interface.

CSS attribute selectors give developers another way to create flexible and maintainable interfaces without adding unnecessary classes to every HTML element.

They are particularly useful for form styling, link identification, and components that already contain meaningful HTML attributes. By choosing precise selectors, understanding matching operators, and testing changes before deployment, developers can use this feature to write cleaner CSS while keeping their markup descriptive and organized.

#10834. SmolVLM - small yet mighty Vision Language Model

This blog post introduces SmolVLM, a 2B VLM, SOTA for its memory footprint. SmolVLM is small, fast, memory-efficient, and fully open-source. All model checkpoints, VLM datasets, training recipes and tools are released under the Apache 2.0 license.

This year has seen a boom in multimodal AI with many large vision language models released. The trends were to initially scale up compute, later scale up the data diversity by generating synthetic data with large models, and, recently, scale down to make these models more efficient. Small open models allow local deployment to browser or edge devices, cut inference costs, and enable user customization. Some notable examples of these models include PaliGemma 3B, moondream2, and Qwen2VL.

In this blog post, we introduce SmolVLM, a new family of 2B small vision language models that can be used commercially and deployed to smaller local setups, with completely open training pipelines.

We release three models: SmolVLM-Base, which can be used for downstream fine-tuning, SmolVLM-Synthetic, the fine-tuned variant on synthetic data, and SmolVLM Instruct, the fine-tuned instruction variant, which can be used out of the box for interactive end-user applications.

This release comes with open-source models integrated into transformers, a demo built on SmolVLM Instruct, and a supervised fine-tuning script. We have used the datasets previously used for Idefics3: the Cauldron and Docmatix, which are also fully open-source.

The Main Building: Located at the center of the complex, the main building features intricate tile work with traditional Thai motifs that cover every inch of the structure. This includes patterns such as dragons, mythical creatures, flowers, and geometric shapes. The roofline has an elaborate design featuring multiple layers of tiles adorned with gold accents.

Towers & Spires: There are several towers within the Grand Palace including the Phra Nakhon Si Ayutthaya National Museum Tower which houses exhibits on Thai culture and heritage. Another notable tower is the Wat Yai Chai Mongkol Tower where you can find beautiful murals depicting scenes from Buddhist mythology.

Architecture Style: The architectural style combines elements of Hindu and Khmer styles seen commonly throughout Southeast Asia. You'll notice influences like stupas (dome-shaped structures), lotus flower carvings, and ornate details typical of these regions' religious buildings.

Visitor Experience: While exploring the Grand Palace, visitors should be aware of certain rules due to security measures taken by authorities. These include no photography inside certain areas or using flashbulbs outside. Additionally, there may be queues during peak tourist seasons so plan accordingly if you're traveling here.

By following these guidelines, your trip will undoubtedly enhance both your understanding of Thailand’s rich historical tapestry and personal enjoyment!

For SmolVLM, we closely followed the architecture from Idefics3, to the point that we use the same implementation in transformers. There are, however a few key differences:

We present benchmarks for the tasks we mention in training details.

SmolVLM provides the best memory usage among the existing suite of vision language models in transformers. This allows it to run efficiently on-device, such as a laptop! You can see above the GPU memory usage in GBs for each model, running inference with one or two input images, and using the same images and text prompts in all tests. SmolVLM's efficiency in image encoding is built into the model. SmolVLM encodes each 384x384 image patch to 81 tokens. This results in SmolVLM encoding our test prompt and a single image in 1.2k tokens, whereas Qwen2-VL uses 16k tokens. This also explains why the memory consumption increases so much for 2 images with Qwen and InternVL. In contrast, the increase is much more moderate for SmolVLM and PaliGemma, which use a similar approach.

SmolVLM's tiny memory footprint also implies that it requires far fewer computations to prefill the model and generate. Compared to Qwen2-VL, the prefill throughput is 3.3 to 4.5 times faster, and the generation throughput is 7.5 to 16 times faster.

Given SmolVLM's long context and the possibility of tweaking the internal frame resizing of the model, we explored its suitability as an accessible option for basic video analysis tasks, particularly when computational resources are limited.

In our evaluation of SmolVLM's video understanding capabilities, we implemented a straightforward video processing pipeline code, extracting up to 50 evenly sampled frames from each video while avoiding internal frame resizing. This simple approach yielded surprisingly competitive results on the CinePile benchmark, with a score of 27.14%, a performance that positions the model between InternVL2 (2B) and Video LlaVa (7B).

The quantitative results align with our qualitative testing, looking at an example from the FineVideo dataset:

While in the second question, we see some temporal understanding limitations (the cook points to one ingredient after the other rather than pointing/holding all of them at the same time) SmolVLM demonstrated great scene understanding and object recognition capabilities.

We integrated SmolVLM with VLMEvalKit to facilitate easy evaluation across additional benchmarks.

By running the following command, you can evaluate SmolVLM or your fine-tuned SmolVLM model.

For example, to evaluate on MMMU dev validation set and MathVista mini and store the results in a folder called smol.

You can easily load SmolVLM using the Auto classes in transformers. Under the hood, the model and processor are mapped to the same implementations used for Idefics3.

Image and text can be interleaved arbitrarily, and you can pass in multiple images. Here’s how you can use the chat template and pass in the formatted input to the processor.

Start generating with preprocessed input and decode the generated output.

First, we had to train SmolLM2 to extend it context, but we will discuss that in the next subsection. Once we had a long context SmolLM2, we trained SmolVLM using the same data that we used for Idefics3. Mainly, we used The Cauldron and Docmatix. The full list of datasets we used can be consulted here.

SmolLM2’s pre-training context window is insufficient for VLMs. Images are encoded into many tokens, and we wanted to support multiple images. To address this, we extended it to 16k tokens by increasing the RoPE base value from 10k to 273k, following the guidelines in “Scaling Laws of RoPE-based Extrapolation”. We fine-tuned the model on a mixture of long- and short-context datasets. For long-context datasets, we used the “books” subset of Dolma (primarily Project Gutenberg) and code documents with 8k+ tokens from The Stack, each contributing 20% to the final mixture. For short-context datasets, we streamlined the original SmolLM2 pre-training mix to include 20% FineWeb-Edu, 20% DCLM, and 20% from our math dataset (to be released soon). The math dataset was upsampled to mitigate a performance drop observed on GSM8k during the context extension process. All experiments were implemented using the EasyContext repository.

For our training run, we saved checkpoints every 25 optimization steps, allowing us to evaluate and potentially recover the model's state at different points in training. This practice is crucial for identifying the optimal model version, as training longer doesn't always guarantee better performance. We evaluated the performance across multiple vision-language benchmarks, each weighted according to their importance. The core benchmarks included the following:

To select the optimal checkpoint, we created a single metric by combining these benchmarks with different manually assigned weights to reflect their relative importance in assessing the model's capabilities. We used this single metric to select the best checkpoint. Generally, the models tended to do great on most benchmarks with more training, but their relative performance on DocVQA would decrease considerably.

You can fine-tune SmolVLM using transformers and apply alignment techniques using TRL 🚀

We provide a notebook to fine-tune it on the VQAv2 dataset, optionally using LoRA, QLoRA or full fine-tuning. In the notebook, you can find some tricks to save up even more memory and have a larger batch size to fit SmolVLM inside consumer GPUs, like L4, for training. With batch sizes of 4, 8-bit loading with QLoRA and gradient checkpointing we can fine-tune in L4, and it consumes around ~16 GBs of VRAM. This makes it possible to fine-tune your SmolVLM using Colab! You can play around with the parameters to get a nice point in training duration-memory trade-off.

SmolVLM also comes with TRL integration so you can apply Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) easily through the CLI. Get started by running pip install trl accelerate peft and then run the following command to fine-tune on RLAIF-V dataset:

The resulting LoRA adapter weights are SmolVLM-Instruct-DPO. A detailed tutorial on preference tuning vision-based LLM can be found here: dpo_vlm.

We introduced SmolVLM, a fully open, small, and mighty VLM for the community! We also provide tools for the community to use and customize it. We are looking forward to seeing what you will create with SmolVLM.

#10833. Rearchitecting Hugging Face Uploads and Downloads

As part of Hugging Face's Xet team’s work to improve Hugging Face Hub’s storage backend, we analyzed a 24 hour window of Hugging Face upload requests to better understand access patterns. On October 11th, 2024, we saw:

The map below visualizes this activity, with countries colored by bytes uploaded per hour.

Currently, uploads are stored in an S3 bucket in us-east-1 and optimized using S3 Transfer Acceleration. Downloads are cached and served using AWS Cloudfront as a CDN. Cloudfront’s 400+ convenient edge locations provide global coverage and low-latency data transfers. However, like most CDNs, it is optimized for web content and has a file size limit of 50GB.

While this size restriction is reasonable for typical internet file transfers, the ever-growing size of files in model and dataset repositories presents a challenge. For instance, the weights of meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-70B total 131GB and are split across 30 files to meet the Hub’s recommendation of chunking weights into 20 GB segments. Additionally, to enable advanced deduplication or compression techniques for both uploads and downloads requires a reimagining of how we handle file transfers.

To push Hugging Face infrastructure beyond its current limits, we are redesigning the Hub’s upload and download architecture. We plan to insert a content-addressed store (CAS) as the first stop for content distribution. This enables us to implement a custom protocol built on a guiding philosophy of dumb reads and smart writes. Unlike Git LFS, which treats files as opaque blobs, our approach analyzes files at the byte level, uncovering opportunities to improve transfer speeds for the massive files found in model and dataset repositories.

The read path prioritizes simplicity and speed to ensure high throughput with minimal latency. Requests for a file are routed to a CAS server, which provides reconstruction information. The data itself remains backed by an S3 bucket in us-east-1, with AWS CloudFront continuing to serve as the CDN for downloads.

The write path is more complex to optimize upload speeds and provide additional security guarantees. Like reads, upload requests are routed to a CAS server, but instead of querying at the file level we operate on chunks. As matches are found, the CAS server instructs the client (e.g., huggingface_hub) to transfer only the necessary (new) chunks. The chunks are validated by CAS before uploading them to S3.

There are many implementation details to address such as network constraints and storage overhead which we’ll cover in future posts. For now, let's look at how reads currently look. The first diagram below show the read and write path as they currently look today:

Meanwhile, in the new design, reads will take the following path:

and finally here is the updated write path:

By managing files at the byte level, we can adapt optimizations to suit different file formats. For instance, we have explored improving the dedupeability of Parquet files, and are now investigating compressing tensor files (e.g., Safetensors) which have the potential to trim 10-25% off upload speeds. As new formats emerge, we are uniquely positioned to develop further enhancements that improve the development experience on the Hub.

This protocol also introduces significant improvements for enterprise customers and power users. Inserting a control plane for file transfers provides added guarantees to ensure malicious or invalid data cannot be uploaded. Operationally, uploads are no longer a black box. Enhanced telemetry provides audit trails and detailed logging, enabling the Hub infrastructure team to identify and resolve issues quickly and efficiently.

To support this custom protocol, we need to determine the optimal geographic distribution for the CAS service. AWS Lambda@Edge was initially considered for its extensive global coverage to help minimize the round-trip time. However, its reliance on Cloudfront triggers made it incompatible with our updated upload path. Instead, we opted to deploy CAS nodes in a select few of AWS’s 34 regions.

Taking a closer look at our 24-hour window of S3 PUT requests, we identified global traffic patterns that reveal the distribution of data uploads to the Hub. As expected, the majority of activity comes from North America and Europe, with continuous, high-volume uploads throughout the day. The data also highlights a strong and growing presence in Asia. By focusing on these core regions, we can place our CAS points of presence to balance storage and network resources while minimizing latency.

While AWS offers 34 regions, our goal is to keep infrastructure costs reasonable while maintaining a high user experience. Out of the 88 countries represented in this snapshot, the Pareto chart above shows that the top 7 countries account for 80% of uploaded bytes, while the top 20 countries contribute 95% of the total upload volume and requests.

The United States emerges as the primary source of upload traffic, necessitating a PoP in this region. In Europe, most activity is concentrated in central and western countries (e.g., Luxembourg, the United Kingdom, and Germany) though there is some additional activity to account for in Africa (specifically Algeria, Egypt, and South Africa). Asia’s upload traffic is primarily driven by Singapore, Hong Kong, Japan, and South Korea.

If we use a simple heuristic to distribute traffic, we can divide our CAS coverage into three major regions:

This ends up being quite effective. The US and Europe account for 78.4% of uploaded bytes, while Asia accounts for 21.6%.

This regional breakdown results in a well-balanced load across our three CAS PoPs, with additional capacity for growth in ap-southeast-1 and flexibility to scale up in us-east-1 and eu-west-3 as needed.

Based on expected traffic, we plan to allocate resources as follows:

Even though we’re increasing the first hop distance for some users, the overall impact to bandwidth across the Hub will be limited. Our estimates predict that while the cumulative bandwidth for all uploads will decrease from 48.5 Mbps to 42.5 Mbps (a 12% reduction), the performance hit will be more than offset by other system optimizations.

We are currently working toward moving our infrastructure into production by the end of 2024, where we will start with a single CAS in us-east-1. From there, we’ll start duplicating internal repositories to our new storage system to benchmark transfer performance, and then replicate our CAS to the additional PoPs mentioned above for more benchmarking. Based on those results, we will continue to optimize our approach to ensure that everything works smoothly when our storage backend is fully in place next year.

As we continue this analysis, new opportunities for deeper insights are emerging. Hugging Face hosts one of the largest collections of data from the open-source machine learning community, providing a unique vantage point to explore the modalities and trends driving AI development around the world.

For example, future analyses could classify models uploaded to the Hub by use case (such as NLP, computer vision, robotics, or large language models) and examine geographic trends in ML activity. This data not only informs our infrastructure decisions but also provides a lens into the evolving landscape of machine learning.

We invite you to explore our current findings in more detail! Visit our interactive Space to see the upload distribution for your region, and follow our team to hear more about what we’re building.

#10832. Open Source Developers Guide to the EU AI Act

The EU AI Act, the world’s first comprehensive legislation on artificial intelligence, has officially come into force, and it’s set to impact the way we develop and use AI – including in the open source community. If you’re an open source developer navigating this new landscape, you’re probably wondering what this means for your projects. This guide breaks down key points of the regulation with a focus on open source development, offering a clear introduction to this legislation and directing you to tools that may help you prepare to comply with it.

Disclaimer: The information provided in this guide is for informational purposes only, and should not be considered as any form of legal advice.

The EU AI Act is a binding regulation that aims to foster responsible AI. To that end, it sets out rules that scale with the level of risk the AI system or model might pose while aiming to preserve open research and support small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). As an open source developer, many aspects of your work won’t be directly impacted – especially if you’re already documenting your systems and keeping track of data sources. In general, there are straightforward steps you can take to prepare for compliance.

The regulation takes effect over the next two years and applies broadly, not just to those within the EU. If you’re an open source developer outside the EU but your AI systems or models are offered or impact people within the EU, they are included in the Act.

The regulation works at different levels of the AI stack, meaning it has different obligations if you are a provider (which includes the developers), deployer, distributor etc. and if you are working on an AI model or system.

In the AI Act, rules scale with the level of risk the AI system or model might pose. For all AI systems, risks may be:

For general purpose AI (GPAI) models, there is another risk category called systemic risk: GPAI models using substantial computing power, today defined as over 10^25 FLOPs for training, or that have high-impact capabilities. According to a study by Stanford, in August 2024, based on estimates from Epoch, only eight models (Gemini 1.0 Ultra, Llama 3.1-405B, GPT-4, Mistral Large, Nemotron-4 340B, MegaScale, Inflection-2, Inflection-2.5) from seven developers (Google, Meta, OpenAI, Mistral, NVIDIA, ByteDance, Inflection) would meet the default systemic risk criterion of being trained using at least 10^25 FLOPs. Obligations vary if they are open source or not.

Our focus in this short guide is on limited risk AI systems and open source non-systemic risk GPAI models, which should encompass most of what is publicly available on the Hub. For other risk categories, make sure to check out further obligations that may apply.

Limited-risk AI systems interact directly with people (end users) and may create risks of impersonation, manipulation, or deception. For example, a chatbot producing text or a text-to-image generator – tools that can also facilitate the creation of misinformation materials or of deepfakes. The AI Act aims to tackle these risks by helping the general end user understand that they are interacting with an AI system. Today, most GPAI models are not considered to present systemic risk. In the case of limited-risk AI systems, the obligations below apply whether or not they are open source.

Developers of limited-risk AI systems need to:

Note that you may also be a ‘deployer’ of an AI system, not only a developer. Deployers of AI systems are people or companies using an AI system in their professional capacity. In that case, you also need to comply with the following:

The information above needs to be provided with clear language, at the latest at the time of the user’s first interaction with, or exposure, to the AI system.

The AI Office, in charge of implementing the AI Act, will help create codes of practice with guidelines for detecting and labeling artificially generated content. These codes are currently being written with industry and civil society participation, and are expected to be published by May 2025. Obligations will be enforced starting August 2026.

The following obligations apply if you are developing open source GPAI models, e.g. LLMs, that do not present systemic risk. Open source for the AI Act means “software and data, including models, released under a free and open source license that allows them to be openly shared and where users can freely access, use, modify and redistribute them or modified versions thereof”. Developers can select from a list of open licenses on the Hub. Check if the chosen license fits the AI Act’s open source definition.

The obligations for non-systemic open source GPAI models are as follows:

The EU AI Act also ties into existing regulations on copyright and personal data, such as copyright directive and data protection regulation. For this, look to Hugging Face-integrated tools that support better opt-out mechanisms and personal data redaction, and stay updated on recommendations from European and national bodies like CNIL.

Projects on Hugging Face have implemented forms of understanding and implementing opt-outs of training data, such as BigCode’s Am I In The Stack app and the integration of a Spawning widget for datasets with image URLs. With these tools, creators can simply opt out of allowing their copyrighted material to be used for AI training. As opt-out processes are being developed to help creators effectively inform publicly that they do not want their content used for AI training, these tools can be quite effective in addressing those decisions.

Developers may rely on codes of practice (which are currently being developed and expected by May 2025) to demonstrate compliance with these obligations.

Other obligations apply if you make your work available in a way that does not meet the criteria for being open source according to the AI Act.

Also, note that if a given GPAI model meets the conditions to pose systemic risks, its developers must notify the EU Commission. In the notification process, developers can argue that their model does not present systemic risks because of specific characteristics. The Commission will review each argument and accept or reject the claim depending on whether the argument is sufficiently substantiated, considering the model’s specific characteristics and capabilities. If the Commission rejects the developers’ arguments, the GPAI model will be designated as posing systemic risk and will need to comply with further obligations, such as providing technical documentation on the model including its training and testing process and the results of its evaluation.

Obligations for GPAI models will be enforced starting August 2025.

Much of the EU AI Act’s practical application is still in development through public consultations and working groups, whose outcome will determine how the Act’s provisions aimed at smoother compliance for SMEs and researchers are operationalized. If you’re interested in shaping how this plays out, now is a great time to get involved!

Thank you, Anna Tordjmann, Brigitte Tousignant, Chun Te Lee, Irene Solaiman, Clémentine Fourrier, Ann Huang, Benjamin Burtenshaw, Florent Daudens for your feedback, comments, and suggestions.

#10831. How to Get a YouTube API Key and Use the Data API (2026)

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

You need a YouTube API key the moment your app has to read anything from YouTube: a video's length, its view count, a channel's latest uploads. Getting one takes about five minutes. Using it well takes a little longer, because YouTube changed how its quota works in June 2026, and plenty of guides still describe the old rules.

In this guide we'll get a key, lock it down and test it. Then we'll use it from Node.js for three real jobs: adding up the length of a playlist, listing a channel's videos without spending a search, and estimating what a video earned. Along the way we'll cover what the YouTube API costs (nothing), how the 2026 quota works, and the errors you're most likely to hit.

A YouTube API key identifies your project to the YouTube Data API v3. With just a key, you can read public data:

A key isn't enough for anything that touches someone's account. Uploading videos, editing playlists or reading private data needs OAuth 2.0, where the user signs in and grants your app access.

You'll need a Google account. The YouTube Data API is free, so there's nothing to pay for.

The restrictions matter more than they look. A key is just a string in a URL, and anyone who copies an unrestricted one can spend your daily quota for you. With an API restriction, the key is useless for other Google APIs. With an application restriction, it only works from your server or your site. Changes to restrictions can take up to five minutes to apply, so don't panic if a request fails straight after you save.

Before writing any code, check the key with a single request. This one asks for the first video ever uploaded to YouTube, and uses the fields parameter to trim the response down to four values:

That request cost 1 unit of your daily quota, which brings us to the question everyone asks.

Yes. There's no charge per request and no paid plan. Instead you get a daily quota, and since June 1, 2026 it's split into separate buckets:

Google's quota calculator lists the cost of every method. Quotas reset at midnight Pacific Time. Every request costs at least 1 unit, including requests that fail, so a retry loop around a broken call can use up a day's quota on its own.

If you've read older guides, search is the big change. A search used to cost 100 units out of the same 10,000, so 100 searches emptied your whole day. Uploads were worse still, at about 1,600 units each until December 2025. Now both have their own buckets, and the 10,000 units are left for everything else.

To give you a feel for what 10,000 units buys, here's what each example in this guide costs:

You can't pay for more. To go above the defaults, fill in the YouTube API Services Audit and Quota Extension Form, which is linked from Google's page on quota and compliance audits. YouTube first audits your project to check it follows the YouTube API Services Terms of Service, then someone from the API team gets back to you. Google doesn't give a timeline, so apply well before you need the extra quota.

Most projects never need to. The rest of this guide is about getting a lot done with very few units.

The examples need Node.js 20.6 or later, for the built-in fetch and the --env-file flag. There are no packages to install. Make a folder with a .env file in it:

Every example imports one small helper. It builds the URL, adds your key and turns API errors into readable messages:

Run any example with node --env-file=.env followed by the file name.

YouTube doesn't tell you how long a playlist is. To work it out, you need two methods:

Durations come back in ISO 8601 format. PT15M33S is 15 minutes 33 seconds, PT1H2M3S adds an hour, and a stream longer than a day looks like P1DT2H3M4S. The toSeconds() function below handles all three.

Here it is on freeCodeCamp's Full Courses in One Video playlist:

That's 184 hours of courses for 4 units of quota. Private and deleted videos still show up in a playlist's items, but videos.list doesn't return them, which is why the script prints "52 of 52 videos available". On a playlist with removed videos, the two numbers will differ.

This is the core of the free YouTube playlist length calculator I built on createthat.ai. The live version adds a target time box that works out the speed you need to finish by a deadline, and it accepts channel, video and Shorts links as well as playlists.

The obvious way to find a channel's videos is to search for them. Don't: search is now capped at 100 calls a day, and it isn't built to list everything a channel has posted. Every channel has an uploads playlist instead, and you can reach it in two cheap calls:

Two units, and none of your 100 daily searches. To get every upload rather than the newest five, page through the playlist with the same pageToken loop as Example 1.

videos.list with part=statistics returns a video's view, like and comment counts. Dislike counts have been private since December 2021 and favoriteCount is always 0, so don't build anything on those. The script also copes with a missing like or comment count, which you'll see on some videos.

This time the fields parameter trims the response to the values we use. That makes the response smaller, but it doesn't change the cost: the call is 1 unit either way.

Here it is on freeCodeCamp's Learn Python full course, one of the most-watched videos in that playlist:

Treat the last line as a rough range, not an answer. The Data API doesn't share anyone's revenue, so any estimate is views multiplied by an RPM: what a creator keeps per 1,000 views. RPM moves a lot with the topic and where the viewers live, and the estimate assumes the video shows ads, which not every channel does.

And sometimes you don't need an API at all. When I built a font tester, I needed a list of Google Fonts. The Google Fonts Developer API would have meant a key and a call on every visit, for a list that barely changes. Instead I generated a file of the 500 most popular fonts once, from Google's public font metadata, and the page loads it like any other file. No key, no quota and nothing to fail.

When a call fails, the response's error.message and error.details[0].reason tell you why. These are the ones you'll see most:

For the invalid key error, the full response looks like this:

Yes. Creating a key and calling the YouTube Data API costs nothing. You're limited by the daily quota instead, and there's no paid tier: more quota comes through an audit.

In the Google Cloud console, select your project and go to APIs & Services > Credentials. Your keys are listed under API keys, with a Show key option next to each one.

It works, but anyone can read the key from your page. If you do it, restrict the key to your website and to the YouTube Data API v3. A small server route that calls the API for you is safer, and it gives you somewhere to cache results.

By default, 100 searches, 100 uploads and 10,000 units for everything else. Most reads cost 1 unit and videos.list takes 50 IDs per call, so that's enough for the details of up to 500,000 videos a day.

Getting a YouTube API key is the easy part: one project, one API to enable, one key and two restrictions. The 2026 quota is generous if you work with it:

All three examples together cost 7 units, out of 10,000. From here, try commentThreads.list to pull a video's comments 100 at a time, or extend Example 2 to page through a channel's entire upload history and add it all up with the code from Example 1.

#10824. Top 6 AI Image Generators in 2026: Features, Strengths, and Limits

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A designer who once spent an afternoon searching stock libraries can now describe the picture they want and have four versions in under a minute. AI image generators have moved from curiosity to everyday tool for blog headers, product mockups, ad concepts, game art and slide decks. The quality gap between tools has narrowed, but the differences that remain matter a lot: how well each follows a detailed prompt, whether it can render readable text, how it handles edits, and what you are allowed to do with the result.

This guide compares six of the best-known options, what each does well and where each falls short. Models, plans and limits change often, so check each vendor's own pages before you commit to a workflow.

OpenArt’s AI image generator puts several image models behind one interface. Its generator page lists models including GPT Image 2.5, Grok Imagine, Qwen Image 3, Nano Banana 2 and Seedream 5.0 Pro, and lets you create images from text prompts or reference photos. It also lists tools for camera angle control, upscaling, collages and a Character Builder for keeping characters consistent across scenes, with 4K export.

Best for: Creators who want to compare several models on the same prompt without juggling separate subscriptions and accounts.

Limitations: The page offers a free start but does not state credit amounts or plan details, and it does not address commercial use, so check the pricing and licensing pages before using results for client work. Output quality depends on which model you pick.

OpenAI's image generation in ChatGPT works inside the chat interface, which makes iteration natural: generate an image, then ask for changes in plain language. OpenAI highlights accurate text rendering, the ability to follow prompts with many distinct objects, and consistent characters across multi-turn edits. You can also upload reference images and have the model transform them. It handles both photorealistic and stylized looks.

Best for: Marketers and writers who want to describe, refine and re-describe an image without learning a new tool.

Limitations: OpenAI notes that tall images such as posters can be cropped too tightly, and that dense small text, multilingual text and precise graphs can still go wrong. Images can take up to a minute to render. All generated images carry C2PA metadata identifying their source.

Gemini's image generation runs on Google's Nano Banana models. Google highlights character consistency, text rendering in many languages, combining several photos, precise editing and 2K resolution. A free tier covers image generation and editing, while the most advanced model requires a Google AI plan. You start from the "Create images" option in the Gemini app, then prompt or upload a picture to edit.

Best for: People who need to keep the same subject across several images, or who want to edit existing photos quickly.

Limitations: Usage limits apply, and the strongest model is behind a paid plan. Images include an invisible SynthID watermark and a visible AI label, which is good for transparency but may not suit every use.

Midjourney is an independent research lab known for images with a strong, painterly look. Its official site points users to a sign-up flow and to a Discord community and help center for support. Many creators choose it for concept art, mood boards and illustration where style matters more than literal accuracy.

Best for: Artists, art directors and game designers who want rich, stylized results and enjoy exploring variations.

Limitations: I could not confirm current pricing, trial terms or feature details from Midjourney's public pages, so check them yourself before subscribing. The workflow can feel less like a normal app than the others on this list, and it is not the easiest route for precise, text-heavy graphics.

Adobe Firefly is built for professionals who already work in Creative Cloud. Adobe states that its Firefly models are commercially safe, trained on licensed Adobe Stock and public domain content, and outputs carry Content Credentials that show AI involvement. It offers text-to-image, image-to-image, sketch-to-image and style transfer, plus editing tools such as background removal, object removal, upscaling and generative expand. It connects with Photoshop, Illustrator, Lightroom and Adobe Express, and also lets you use partner models from other companies.

Best for: Designers and brand teams who need clear licensing and want AI inside the apps they already use.

Limitations: Plans work on a credit system, so heavy use adds up. Adobe lists a free tier with limited daily generations and paid plans starting at about $9.99 a month, but confirm current terms on its site.

Ideogram built its reputation on a problem that trips up many generators: readable text. Its current models are presented as producing clean typography in different layouts, with attention to prompt fidelity and reliable editing. It also offers an API with access to a catalog of models, and has released open weights for one earlier model for local use and customization under its license.

Best for: Posters, social graphics, logo concepts and anything where words are part of the image.

Limitations: The pages I checked did not describe a free plan, so look at current plans before relying on it. Like every generator, it still needs a human to proofread the text it produces.

Start with the job. If you want to compare several models side by side, try OpenArt. If you want to talk your way to a finished image, try ChatGPT or Gemini. If you need images that will sit inside a branded design workflow, Firefly is the safer fit. If you are chasing a distinctive look, Midjourney deserves a trial. If text must be perfect, test Ideogram.

Run the same prompt in two or three tools before paying. Differences in composition, hands, faces and text show up quickly, and they matter more than any feature list.

Reviews only go so far, because your own use case is what counts. Pick one realistic job, for example a 16:9 header image for a blog post about web performance, and run the same prompt through two or three tools. Write the prompt once and paste it unchanged, so the comparison is fair:

Then score each result on five questions: Did it follow every instruction? Are there odd details in hands, edges or objects? Is any text spelled correctly? Does it still look good when cropped to a square? Could you license it for your project? Ten minutes of this teaches more than any feature list, and it shows how much editing each tool needs before you can publish.

Most readers of this guide will put these images on web pages, where a few habits matter more than the generator you choose.

There is no single best AI image generator. The right pick depends on whether you value conversation, style, licensing, control or typography. Test two or three on a real project, compare the output, and keep a human in charge of the final choice. Whatever you generate, review it for errors and label AI-made images clearly where your audience would expect it.

Are AI-generated images free to use commercially? It depends on the provider and your plan. Read the licensing terms for the tool you use, and consider vendors that publish how their models were trained if you work for clients.

Which AI image generator is best for text in images? Ideogram and ChatGPT both highlight text rendering, and Gemini lists it as a feature. Test each with your own wording and proofread the result.

Do AI images have watermarks? Some do. OpenAI adds C2PA metadata, Google adds an invisible SynthID watermark and a visible label, and Adobe attaches Content Credentials.

Can I use more than one image model without separate accounts? Yes. Platforms such as OpenArt put several models in one interface, which makes side-by-side testing easier. Check the licensing terms for each model you use.

Should I add alt text to AI-generated images? Yes, when the image carries meaning. Describe what it shows or why it is there. Purely decorative images can use an empty alt attribute, following the W3C guidance.

#10817. SEO For AI Crawlers: How to serve AI Agent friendly pages?

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

AI-friendly pages are plain-text (usually markdown) versions of webpages that are meant for AI, rather than people. Websites typically determine that AI is requesting a page via the user agent, Accept header, or a specific .md URL.

We ran this test at acme.bot on November 4, 2026, across 53 live pages on 43 host names. Because we targeted sites likely to do this, the sample leans towards developer tools.

While testing the HubSpot, Gymshark, Semrush and Profound web pages, we didn't find any markdown on the pages.

While it's a common practice in developer documentation, there's not much research or evidence that it helps AI visibility.

Dries Buytaert checked a month of Cloudflare logs and found no AI crawler using content negotiation. The crawlers reached his markdown only through dedicated URLs, by following an auto-discovery link. So a site that relies on Accept alone is serving coding agents - and, possibly, no crawlers at all.

Even when the request asks for HTML, Stripe's docs still send markdown to all six AI user agents we tested. They send HTML to Bingbot, Googlebot, and browsers. The Checkout page drops from 846 KB to 5.5 KB. Its markdown has links to other .md pages, keeping an agent in the text pages. The response to markdown comes with the header X-Robots-Tag: none to ensure it is kept out of search indexes. Sentry's docs route the same way.

Vercel pages (including the blog and pricing page) that we tried all returned markdown on request. Docs pages also go to AI user agents, unless the request prefers HTML. Pricing and blog pages do not. The Next.js docs exhibit a similar behavior.

Neon delivers markdown on docs and pricing to non-browser clients that do not prefer HTML, including plain curl.

Neon's page isn't just a conversion. The markdown copy of its introduction is about 3,070 words, against roughly 620 in the visible HTML, and it speaks directly to the agent: "The user needs a Neon account." This sentence, however, is not in the HTML. Linear has a smaller version, which opens its markdown with a line that starts "For agents" and points to its MCP server.

Neon's markdown has Vary: Accept, User-Agent and X-Robots-Tag: noindex headers.

Cloudflare's Markdown for Agents converts HTML to markdown on the fly, without needing any work on an origin server. It's available on the Pro plan and above and handles up to 6 MiB of HTML. Cloudflare reports one post falling from 16,180 tokens to 3,150.

1. Fix the HTML first. Vercel's guide says it plainly: "Make the HTML work before adding a Markdown mirror." Render the content on the server, because many AI crawlers don't run JS.

2. Generate markdown from the same source as the HTML. That keeps the two versions in step when the page changes.

3. Answer Accept: text/markdown. Return Content-Type: text/markdown; charset=utf-8 at the same URL, with a fallback to HTML when there's no markdown.

4. Publish .md URLs and link to them. Each page should have a added to it. In Buytaert's logs, this is the route the crawlers took.

5. Add user agent detection only if you need it. Identify the agents you want to serve, and omit search engines. Should the list include training crawlers? Stripe's does and Mintlify's doesn't. Since user agents can be faked, use the crawler IP ranges that Anthropic and OpenAI publish to check logs.

6. Set the cache key. Send Vary: Accept, and also User-Agent if it determines the response. Otherwise, a shared cache can give a person the markdown.

7. Keep the markdown out of search results. Use either a Link header to canonicalize the page to the HTML or add an X-Robots-Tag: noindex header.

8. Log the Accept header. You can't measure it if you don't record it, and many servers don't record it by default.

The evidence of benefit is thin, and it measures crawling, not citations.

Google's John Mueller called converting pages "such a stupid idea". He also questioned whether crawlers would be able to follow links written in markdown. Bing's Fabrice Canel cautioned that non-user versions "are often neglected, broken."

Google's spam policies define cloaking as a website showing different content to Googlebot than it would to users. In our controlled test, all sites kept Googlebot on HTML. We found no Google document that rules on content negotiation or on markdown sent only to AI crawlers.

If your site is developer documentation, making you site agent friendly is cheap, and your readers' coding agents already ask for it. So, answer Accept: text/markdown requests and publish linked .md URLs. Keep both out of the index.

For a marketing site, the case is not that strong. No study yet shows more AI citations, and maintaining two copies of every page over time will be an overhead.

If citations are the goal, freshness looks like a stronger lever than format. In our study of 356 cited pages for getting cited by ChatGPT, typical article was two years old - but seven in ten had been edited in the last year.

#10811. Which MCM Has the Best Revshare? A Developer’s Guide to Evaluating Ad Partners

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

An ad partner’s revenue share looks easy to compare: keeping 90% sounds better than keeping 80%. But the percentage does not tell a developer what will happen when the integration reaches production. Extra JavaScript, unstable ad slots, opaque reporting, and difficult rollbacks can change the value of an apparently attractive deal.

For teams maintaining an advertising-funded website, choosing a Multiple Customer Management (MCM) partner is partly an engineering decision. The integration affects page templates, consent handling, third-party requests, account access, and monitoring. Those changes deserve the same scrutiny as a new analytics SDK or payment integration.

This guide explains how to compare revenue shares on a consistent basis, review integration requirements, and test an ad setup without sacrificing usability. The goal is a repeatable evaluation process, rather than a universal winner.

Google Ad Manager’s MCM system lets a parent publisher manage a child publisher’s account or delegated inventory. The commercial agreement defines the partner’s services and compensation. Before comparing offers, ask which revenue streams the quoted percentage covers and whether the reporting figure is before or after that fee.

Use three separate lines in your evaluation spreadsheet:

Revenue base: record the amount to which the partner’s percentage applies. Advertiser spending, exchange-reported revenue, and publisher earnings are different figures. Do not treat them as interchangeable.

Partner compensation: identify the percentage, fixed charges, and any optional services. Ask whether the same terms apply to every demand source and ad format.

Adjustments: distinguish estimated revenue from finalized earnings, including invalid-traffic deductions and other corrections. Document when adjustments appear and which party bears them.

A common mistake is applying the partner fee twice because a dashboard already displays net revenue. Label each exported metric before using it in a comparison.

The two delegation models have different implications for access, reporting, and payments. Google’s documentation is the starting point for checking the proposed setup.

Manage Account gives the parent edit access within the child’s account while the child retains access and permissions. Payment facilitation can allocate eligible earnings from the child’s primary Ad Exchange account, but it does not automatically cover every third-party revenue stream. Confirm the invitation’s payment percentage and the separate commercial agreement.

Manage Inventory lets the parent manage delegated inventory in its own account, without access to the child account. Reporting for that inventory sits in the parent account. Google pays the parent for the relevant inventory, and the parent pays the child according to their agreement. Ask how you will obtain reports and reconcile payments.

Before implementation, document who can change tags, ad units, consent settings, and demand configuration. Agree on access for debugging and exporting historical data. A developer should be able to trace a production request to its configuration owner.

Use this table as a request-for-information checklist. It does not rank providers or assert that any named service supports a particular implementation. Obtain current terms and technical documentation for the product you are considering.

Apply the same standards to every proposal. The following examples show what a developer should ask during evaluation; each question is relevant across providers.

MonetizeMore offers publisher monetization products, including PubGuru and Traffic Cop. When evaluating its proposal, connect the commercial discussion to concrete integration questions: which scripts will load, who owns the configuration, and how will reported earnings be reconciled?

Request a sample report showing the revenue base, partner fee, and deductions as separate fields. Check whether the proposed plan includes every service shown in the sales demonstration.

Ask for a written ownership map covering Ad Manager access, tag deployment, configuration changes, and incident response. Identify who can restore the previous setup if delivery fails.

During a trial, compare representative templates and devices. Record script requests and main-thread activity alongside net revenue, using the same measurement definitions for the existing setup.

Decision criterion: choose on measured results and documented responsibilities, rather than assuming that a quoted split predicts final earnings.

For any proposal involving a header-bidding wrapper, including one from Setupad, ask how the wrapper fits into your existing page lifecycle.

Review bidder configuration, auction timeouts, and when the ad server receives targeting information. A missing bid and an unfilled ad slot are different problems.

Check whether your team can inspect the active configuration and reproduce an issue on a test page. Agree on who approves changes to bidders or timeout values.

Measure the complete sequence: consent readiness, auction start, bid responses, ad request, and rendering. Avoid attributing every delay to the same component.

Decision criterion: the implementation should be observable enough to explain failures, with commercial terms verified separately.

When assessing Publisher Collective or another managed partner, establish how the proposed setup could be tested on a limited, agreed scope.

Ask whether rollout can be restricted to selected templates or an eligible traffic cohort. Do not assume partial testing is available until the partner confirms it.

Record device, geography, page type, and consent state so differences in traffic mix do not masquerade as a revenue improvement.

Keep a dated deployment log connecting each configuration version with the reporting period.

Decision criterion: a measured comparison should separate implementation changes from changes in audience or demand.

A proposal from AdPushup or another optimization provider may involve changes to ad placement. Review the actual proposed changes with both design and engineering.

Check spacing, responsive behavior, keyboard navigation, and whether sticky placements obscure content or controls.

Reserve space for expected ad dimensions and test what happens when no ad is returned.

Compare layout stability before and after the change.

Decision criterion: additional earnings should be assessed alongside usability and performance, with explicit acceptance criteria.

For an Ezoic proposal, as for any managed platform, start with the exact integration method offered to your site.

List required changes to scripts, plugins, caching, DNS, or delivery infrastructure, if any. Do not assume that every deployment uses the same method.

Test interactions with your consent manager, content security policy, caching rules, and existing analytics.

Document how to remove the integration and restore the prior configuration.

Decision criterion: the operational cost should be visible before the first production rollout.

When reviewing a Monumetric proposal, establish which implementation work belongs to your team and which belongs to the provider.

Ask who creates ad slots, updates templates, and validates responsive sizes.

Request a support escalation process with the diagnostic information required for an incident: URL, timestamp, device, consent state, and affected slot.

Confirm onboarding costs and payment terms in writing.

Decision criterion: routine changes and production failures should have a clear owner.

Chrome DevTools helps trace third-party requests in the Network panel and investigate long tasks in the Performance panel. Capture a baseline before deployment, then repeat the same navigation and interaction sequence after deployment. Use comparable device and network settings.

Google Publisher Console helps investigate Google Publisher Tag ad slots and delivery issues. For a Prebid-based setup, use Prebid’s debugging tools to inspect the auction path. These tools answer different questions: whether the auction behaved as expected and whether the ad server delivered the requested slot.

PageSpeed Insights provides performance diagnostics; distinguish its lab results from available field data. Add web-vitals to your own monitoring when you need measurements associated with a deployment or cohort. Track LCP, INP, and CLS alongside revenue instead of treating a single Lighthouse score as the complete user experience.

Reserve responsive space for ad slots before content arrives, and investigate shifts when empty slots collapse. SitePoint’s guide to web performance optimization explains related techniques for loading JavaScript, reducing layout work, and managing long tasks.

With the same traffic volume, revenue definition, and deduction rate, the break-even increase in pre-partner revenue is: (current publisher share ÷ new publisher share) − 1. Express shares consistently as fractions or percentages. The table below shows the required lift; it is not a forecast these thresholds only describe the arithmetic. Different ad density, audience mix, deduction rates, or reporting bases can invalidate the comparison. Normalize to the same denominator, such as revenue per thousand pageviews, and compare matched periods or properly assigned concurrent cohorts.

Assume two hypothetical setups each receive one million pageviews. Here, RPM means revenue per thousand pageviews before the partner fee. For this simplified example, deductions reduce that revenue before the publisher share is applied.

Partner A: $10 pre-partner RPM × 1,000 groups of pageviews × 0.90 after deductions × 0.90 publisher share = $8,100 net revenue.

Partner B: $12 pre-partner RPM × 1,000 groups of pageviews × 0.98 after deductions × 0.80 publisher share = $9,408 net revenue.

The difference is $1,308 for the period despite Partner B’s lower share. These are illustrative inputs, not provider performance claims. Faster payment improves cash-flow timing; it does not, by itself, increase the revenue earned.

Use Playwright with mocked responses or test creatives in a controlled environment to check slow loading, empty slots, blocked scripts, and navigation between routes. Verify that the page remains usable when the ad system fails. Automated tests should not click live advertisements or generate artificial monetized traffic.

Separate unit tests for configuration logic, integration tests for component boundaries, and browser tests for user-visible behavior. SitePoint’s explanation of unit, functional, and integration testing provides a useful foundation. Define rollback criteria before launch, keep the control configuration available, and review finalized revenue alongside performance data before expanding the deployment.

There is no universal answer from the percentage alone. Compare current written offers using the same revenue base, then evaluate finalized net earnings, performance, access, and implementation effort.

Not necessarily. Reports may differ in timezone, currency, transaction coverage, fee treatment, and finalization date. Reconcile those definitions before treating a discrepancy as an integration bug.

Ask how renewals, volume tiers, optional services, and rate changes are handled. Record the applicable terms with the configuration and reporting period used for your evaluation.

No. If deductions and the revenue base are otherwise comparable, an 80% share needs 12.5% more pre-partner revenue to match a 90% share. Measure whether that lift exists rather than assuming it.

Do not treat any protection claim as a guarantee. Ask how suspected invalid traffic is handled, what evidence is available, and how later adjustments are reflected in your reports and payments.

Choose the setup that produces verifiable net value while meeting the site’s performance and operational requirements. A good evaluation leaves your team with reproducible measurements, understandable reports, and a practical rollback plan—not just a favorable percentage.
